---
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{do}
$p_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} p$ if and only if there are a directed upward $\varnothing\ne Q\subseteq P$ and a directed downward $\varnothing\ne R\subseteq P$ such that $\bigvee Q=p=\bigwedge R$ and for every $q\in Q$ and $r\in R$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $p_{\alpha}\in\left[q,r\right]$, as soon as $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For necessity it is enough to take $Q:=\left\{q_{\beta}\right\}_{\beta\in B}$ and $R:=\left\{r_{\beta}\right\}_{\beta\in B}$. For sufficiency, let $B:=Q\times R^{\mathrm{op}}$, and for $\beta=\left(q,r\right)\in B$ define $q_{\beta}:=q$, and $r_{\beta}:=r$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{oco}
Every order preserving map that preserves all suprema and infima (resp. extrema of monotone nets) is order (resp. directed order) continuous. The identity map is order- and directed order continuous from $\left(P,\le\right)$ into $\left(P,\ge\right)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{oc}
A net $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq P$ order converges to $p\in P$ if and only if
\[\bigvee \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}=p=\bigwedge \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}.\]
In particular, order limits are unique. Order intervals and principal upper and lower sets are closed with respect to order convergence.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Sufficiency: Take $Q:=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}$ and $R:=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$. We only need to show that they are nonempty. Indeed, if $Q=\varnothing$, then $p=\bigvee \varnothing$ implies that $p$ is the least element of $P$, and so in particular, $p\in Q$, contradiction. Similarly, $R\ne\varnothing$.

Necessity: Let $Q,R$ be as in the definition of order convergence. Since we have that $Q\subseteq \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}\le \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$, it follows that $Q\le \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$, and since $\bigvee Q=p$ we conclude that $p\le \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$. This together with $R\subseteq \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$ and $\bigwedge R=p$ yields $p= \bigwedge\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}$. The other equality is proved similarly.

For the last claim assume that $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq\left[q\right)$, for some $q\in P$. Then, $q\in \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}$, from where $p=\bigvee \left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}\ge q$. Hence, $\left[q\right)$ is order closed, and similarly $\left(q\right]$ is also order closed. For $p\le q$ we have that $\left[p,q\right]=\left[p\right)\cap \left(q\right]$ is order closed as an intersection of order closed sets.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
If $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq P$ is increasing, then $p=\bigvee p_{\alpha}$ if and only if $p_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} p$ if and only if $p_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} p$ (and the same for decreasing nets and infimum).
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The direct implications are straightforward. Assume that $p_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} p$. For every $\alpha\in A$ we have that $p_{\alpha}\le p_{\beta}$, for each $\beta\ge\alpha$, and as the tail $\left(p_{\beta}\right)_{\beta\ge\alpha}\subseteq\left[p_{\alpha}\right)$ order converges to $p$, by Proposition~\ref{oc} we have $p\in \left[p_{\alpha}\right)$. Hence, $p\ge p_{\alpha}$, for every $\alpha\in A$. Assume that $q\ge p_{\alpha}$, for every $\alpha\in A$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{oc}, $\left(q\right]\ni p_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} p$ yields $p\le q$. Hence, $p=\bigvee p_{\alpha}$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
A directed order limit is unique. Order intervals and principal upper and lower sets are directed order closed.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{ocp}
If $Q\subseteq P$ is supremum- and infimum-dense, then the embedding from $Q$ into $P$ preserves all suprema and infima and is directed order continuous. Moreover, order convergence in $Q$ coincides with order convergence in $P$ restricted to $Q$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First, let us prove that the inclusion map from $Q$ into $P$ preserves all suprema and infima. Assume that $r\in Q$ and $R\subseteq Q$ are such that $r=\bigvee_{Q} R$. If $p\in P$ is such that $p\ge R$, then for every $q\in \left[p\right)_{Q}$ we have $R\le p\le q$, therefore $r\le q$; hence $\left[p\right)_{Q}\ge r$, from where $p=\bigwedge\left[p\right)_{Q}\ge r$. As $p$ was chosen arbitrarily, we conclude that $r=\bigvee_{P} R$. Similarly, if $r=\bigwedge_{Q} R$, then $r=\bigwedge_{P} R$. By virtue of Proposition~\ref{oco} we conclude that the inclusion map is order- and directed order continuous.

On the other hand, assume that $\left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq Q$ order converges in $P$ to $q\in Q$, that is, $\bigvee \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{P}}=q=\bigwedge \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow_{P}}$. For every $p\in \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{P}}$ we have that $\left(p\right]_{Q}\subseteq \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{Q}}$ and $p=\bigvee\left(p\right]_{Q}$. It follows that
\[\left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{Q}}=\bigcup_{p\in \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{P}}}\left(p\right]_{Q},\quad\text{and so}\quad \bigvee \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{Q}}=\bigvee_{p\in \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow_{P}}}\left(p\right]_{Q}=q\]
(supremum in $P$, hence in $Q$), and similarly $q=\bigwedge \left(q_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow_{Q}}$. Thus, $q_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} q$ in $Q$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{dcoc}
If $P$ is a Dedekind complete lattice, then a net $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ order converges to $p\in P$ if and only if there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $\left\{p_{\alpha}\right\}_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}$ is order bounded and
\[\bigwedge_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}\bigvee_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta}=p=\bigvee_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta}.\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{macneille}
Order convergence in $P$ is the restriction of order convergence in $P^{\partial}$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
If $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq P$, then:
\item[(i)] $\bigwedge_{\alpha}\bigvee_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow}$ in $P^{\partial}$.
\item[(ii)] $\bigwedge_{\alpha}\bigvee_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow}$ in $\left(P^{\partial}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}$.
\item[(iii)] There is an order limit of $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ in $P^{\partial}$ if and only if there is one in $\left(P^{\partial}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}$ if and only if $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow\downarrow}$ if and only if $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow\uparrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow}$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(i): Let $J$ be the embedding from $P$ into $P^{\partial}$ via $p\mapsto\left(p\right]$, and let $I\colon P\to \left(P^{\partial}\right)^{\mathrm{op}}$ be defined via $p\mapsto\left[p\right)$. Note that $I$ is order reversing. For every $\alpha$ we have that $\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}Jp_{\beta}=\bigcap_{\beta\ge\alpha}\left(p_{\beta}\right]$. Hence, in $P^{\partial}$ we have
\[\bigvee_{\alpha}\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}Jp_{\beta}=\left(\bigcup_{\alpha}\bigcap_{\beta\ge\alpha}\left(p_{\beta}\right]\right)^{\uparrow\downarrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow\downarrow}.\]
Similarly, $\bigvee_{\alpha}\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}Ip_{\beta}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow\uparrow}$.
Now
\[\bigwedge_{\alpha}\bigvee_{\beta\ge\alpha}Jp_{\beta}=\left(\bigvee_{\alpha}\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}Ip_{\beta}\right)^{\downarrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow}.\]

(ii) is proved similarly.

(iii): It follows from Corollary~\ref{dcoc} that there is an order limit of $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ in $P^{\partial}$ if and only if
\[\bigwedge_{\alpha}\bigvee_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta}=\bigvee_{\alpha}\bigwedge_{\beta\ge\alpha}p_{\beta},\]
which is equivalent to $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow\downarrow}$, and also equivalent to $\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow\downarrow\uparrow}=\left(p_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow\uparrow}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{pat}
Let $P=\left\{\left(0,t\right): 0\le t\le 1\right\}\cup \left\{\left(t,0\right): 0\le t\le 1\right\}\cup\left\{\left(1,1\right)\right\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ define $p_{n}:=\left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right)$ and $q_{n}:=\left(\frac{1}{n},0\right)$. We have $p_{n},q_{n}\downarrow \left(0,0\right)$, hence $p_{n},q_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} \left(0,0\right)$ and $p_{n},q_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} \left(0,0\right)$, but the only eventual upper bound for $p_{1},q_{1},p_{2},q_{2},\dots$ is $\left(1,1\right)$, which means that the sequence does not order converge (and hence does not directed order converge) to $\left(0,0\right)$.
\qed
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{sum}
If $P,Q\subseteq E$ with $g=\bigwedge P$ and $h=\bigwedge Q$, then $g+h=\bigwedge\left(P+Q\right)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
It is easy to see that $g+h\le P+Q$. If $e\in E$ is such that $e\le P+Q$, then, for every $p\in P$ and $q\in Q$ we have that $e-p\le q$. Hence, $e-p\le Q$, from where $e-p\le h$, or $e-h\le P$. Thus, $e-h\le g$, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{ocv}
\item[(i)] A net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ converges in order to $e\in E$ if and only if there is $P\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ which dominates the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}-e\right)_{\alpha\in A}$, i.e.\ for each $p\in P$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $-p\le e_{\alpha}-e\le p$, as soon as $\alpha\ge \alpha_{0}$.
\item[(ii)] Addition and taking the additive inverse are order continuous operations on $E$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
(i): $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$ if and only if there are $Q,R\subseteq E$ with $\bigvee Q=e=\bigwedge R$, and such that for every $q\in Q$ and $r\in R$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $\left\{e_{\alpha}\right\}_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}\subseteq\left[q,r\right]$. Note that if $f\in\left[q,r\right]$, then $q-r\le f-e\le r-q$. Hence, $P:=R-Q$ dominates the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}-e\right)_{\alpha\in A}$, and satisfies $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ by Lemma~\ref{sum}.

Conversely, if $P$ dominates the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}-e\right)_{\alpha\in A}$, let $Q:=e-P$ and $R:=e+P$. Clearly, $\bigvee Q=e=\bigwedge R$. If $q\in Q$ and $r\in R$, there are $g,h\in P$ such that $q=e-g$ and $r=e+h$. Find $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ such that $-g\le e_{\alpha}-e\le g$, for every $\alpha\ge \alpha_{1}$, and $-h\le e_{\alpha}-e\le h$, for every $\alpha\ge \alpha_{2}$. Take $\alpha_{0}\ge\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$. For every $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$ we have $q=e-g\le e_{\alpha}\le e+h=r$.

(ii): Assume that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$ and $f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} f$, which is witnessed by $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Using Lemma~\ref{sum}, it is easy to show that $P+Q$ witnesses $e_{\alpha}+f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e+f$. Order continuity of the map $e\mapsto -e$ is straightforward.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{ocauchy}
For a net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is order Cauchy;
\item[(ii)] There are $Q,R\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge \left(R-Q\right)=0_{E}$ and such that for all $q\in Q$ and $r\in R$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $e_{\alpha}\in\left[q,r\right]$, as soon as $\alpha\ge \alpha_{0}$;
\item[(iii)] $\bigwedge\left(\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\nearrow}-\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}^{\searrow}\right)=0_{E}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Let $P\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ dominate the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\right)_{\alpha,\beta\in A}$, so that for every $p\in P$ we can choose $\alpha_{p}\in A$ such that $-p\le e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\le p$, as soon as $\alpha,\beta\ge\alpha_{p}$. For all $p,q\in P$ we can find $\alpha\ge \alpha_{p},\alpha_{q}$; then $e_{\alpha_{p}}-e_{\alpha_{q}}=e_{\alpha_{p}}-e_{\alpha}+e_{\alpha}-e_{\alpha_{q}}\le p+q$, from where $e_{\alpha_{p}}-p\le e_{\alpha_{q}}+q$. Then, $Q:=\left\{e_{\alpha_{p}}-p:p\in P\right\}$ and $R:=\left\{e_{\alpha_{p}}+p:p\in P\right\}$ satisfy $\bigwedge \left(R-Q\right)=0_{E}$. Moreover, for $p,q\in P$ and $\alpha\ge\alpha_{p},\alpha_{q}$ we have $e_{\alpha_{p}}-p\le e_{\alpha}\le e_{\alpha_{q}}+q$, hence $Q, R$ are as required.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is proved similarly to Proposition~\ref{ocv}. (ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii) is proved similarly to Proposition~\ref{oc}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{todovs}
\item[(i)] A net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ directed order converges to $e\in E$ if and only if there is a downward directed $P\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ which dominates the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}-e\right)_{\alpha\in A}$.
\item[(ii)] If for a net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ there are an upward directed $Q\subseteq E$ and a downward directed $R\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge \left(R-Q\right)=0_{E}$ such that for all $q\in Q$ and $r\in R$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $e_{\alpha}\in\left[q,r\right]$, as soon as $\alpha\ge \alpha_{0}$, then this net is directed order Cauchy.
\item[(iii)] Addition and taking the additive inverse are directed order continuous on $E$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{docont}
If $E$ and $F$ are ordered vector spaces, then a positive linear map $T\colon E\to F$ is directed order continuous if and only if for any $P\subseteq E$ with $P\downarrow 0_{E}$ it follows that $TP\downarrow 0_{F}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{arch0}
If an ordered vector space $F$ contains an Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ as a supremum-dense subspace, then $F$ is Archimedean.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $f\in F_{+}$. There is $e\in E$ such that $e\ge f$. Assume that $h\in F$ is such that $h\le \frac{1}{n}f$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, for every $g\in E$ such that $g\le h$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we have $g\le h\le \frac{1}{n}f\le \frac{1}{n}e$. Since $E$ is Archimedean, it follows that $g\le 0_{E}$. Then, $h=\bigvee\left(h\right]_{E}\le 0_{F}$, which shows that $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{1}{n}f=0_{F}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{arch}Assume that $E$ is Archimedean and $\varnothing\ne Q\subseteq E$ is bounded from below. Then:
\item[(i)] If $f\in E$ is such that $Q-f\subseteq Q$, then $f\le0_{E}$.
\item[(ii)] $\bigwedge \left(Q-Q^{\downarrow}\right)=0_{E}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First, by shifting $Q$ if needed we may assume that $Q\subseteq E_{+}$.

(i): Since $Q$ is nonempty, there is $g\in Q$. Then, $g-f\in Q$. Arguing by induction, it follows that $g-nf\in Q\subseteq E_{+}$, hence
$g\ge nf$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. As $E$ is Archimedean, we conclude that $f\le 0_{E}$.

(ii): First, $0_{E}\in Q^{\downarrow}$, and so $Q^{\downarrow}\ne\varnothing$; moreover $Q\ge Q^{\downarrow}$, hence $Q- Q^{\downarrow}\subseteq E_{+}$. Assume that $e\in E$ is such that $Q-Q^{\downarrow}\ge e$. Then, for every $g\in Q$ and $h\in Q^{\downarrow}$ it follows that $g-h\ge e$, from where $g\ge h+e$, and so $h+e\in Q^{\downarrow}$. Hence, $Q^{\downarrow}+e\subseteq Q^{\downarrow}$. Since $Q^{\downarrow}$ is bounded from above, it is easy to deduce from (i) that $e\le 0_{E}$, and so the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{rucauchy}
A net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ is relatively uniformly Cauchy if and only if there are $h\in E_{+}$, and sequences $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\left(g_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq E$ and $\left(\alpha_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq A$ such that $f_{n}\le f_{n+1}$, $g_{n+1}\le g_{n}$, $g_{n}-f_{n}\le\frac{1}{n}h$, and $f_{n}\le e_{\alpha}\le g_{n}$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
It is easy to see that if the conditions in the proposition are satisfied, then the net $\left(e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\right)_{\alpha,\beta\in A}$ is relatively uniformly null with regulator $h$. Hence, we only need to prove the converse. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $\alpha_{n}\in A$ such that $-\frac{1}{2^{n}}h\le e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\le \frac{1}{2^{n}}h$, for every $\alpha,\beta\ge\alpha_{n}$. Furthermore, we may assume that $\left(\alpha_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is increasing.

Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and define $f_{n}:=e_{\alpha_{n}}-\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}h$ and $g_{n}:=e_{\alpha_{n}}+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}h$. For $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$ we have $-\frac{1}{2^{n}}h\le e_{\alpha}-e_{\alpha_{n}}\le \frac{1}{2^{n}}h$, hence $f_{n}\le e_{\alpha_{n}}-\frac{1}{2^{n}}h\le e_{\alpha}\le e_{\alpha_{n}}+\frac{1}{2^{n}}h\le g_{n}$. In particular, $f_{n}+\frac{1}{2^{n}}h=e_{\alpha_{n}}-\frac{1}{2^{n}}h\le e_{\alpha_{n+1}}$, hence $f_{n}\le e_{\alpha_{n+1}}-\frac{1}{2^{n}}h=f_{n+1}$ and similarly $g_{n+1}\le g_{n}$. Finally, $g_{n}-f_{n}=\frac{1}{2^{n-2}}h$, and so with some relabelling it is easy to achieve the desired condition.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{oca}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is Archimedean;
\item[(ii)] Directed order convergence is weaker than relative uniform convergence;
\item[(iii)] Order convergence is weaker than relative uniform convergence;
\item[(iv)] Any increasing bounded from above net is order Cauchy.\medskip

If, additionally, $E$ is directed, then order convergence in $E$ is the restriction of order convergence in $E^{\delta}$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) follows from the fact that if $h$ is a regulator of convergence for a net, then $\left\{\frac{1}{n}h\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ witnesses directed order convergence of this net. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) follows from $\mathrm{o}\le\mathrm{do}$. (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) follows from the facts that $\left(\frac{1}{n}h\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is relatively uniformly null, for every $h\in E_{+}$, and that the order limit of a decreasing net is its infimum.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(iv): Let $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ be an order bounded increasing net in $E$, let $Q:=\left\{e_{\alpha}\right\}_{\alpha\in A}$ and let $R:=Q^{\uparrow}$. It can be deduced from part~(ii) of Lemma~\ref{arch} that $\bigwedge\left(R-Q\right)=0_{E}$. Hence, according to Proposition~\ref{ocauchy}, the net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is order Cauchy.

(iv)$\Rightarrow$(i): Fix $h\in E_{+}$ and consider the order bounded decreasing sequence $\left(\frac{1}{n}h\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, which is order Cauchy by (iv). It follows that there is $P\subseteq E$ such that $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ and for every $p\in P$ there is $n_{p}$ so that $\left|\frac{1}{n}h-\frac{1}{m}h\right|\le p$, for all $m,n\ge n_{p}$. In particular, taking $n:=n_{p}$ and $m:=2n_{p}$ yields $\frac{1}{2n_{p}}h\le p$. We now conclude from $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ that $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{1}{n}h=0_{E}$. Thus, $E$ is Archimedean.

The last claim follows immediately from Proposition~\ref{ocp}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
A directed Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ is complete with respect to order convergence if and only if it is closed with respect to order convergence in $E^{\delta}$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{monc}
\item[(i)] Every monotone complete ordered vector space is Archimedean and relatively uniformly complete. In such spaces any net which satisfies the conditions of part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{todovs} is directed order convergent.
\item[(ii)] Every Archimedean ordered vector space which is complete with respect to order convergence is monotone complete and directed order complete.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
(i): Every monotone order bounded net has an extremum, hence is order convergent, and so order Cauchy. This implies the Archimedean property by Proposition~\ref{oca}.

Assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ is relatively uniformly Cauchy and let $h\in E_{+}$, $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$,\ $\left(g_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq E$ and $\left(\alpha_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq A$ be as in Proposition~\ref{rucauchy}. Since $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\left(g_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ are monotone and order bounded, there are $f,g\in E$ such that $f_{n}\uparrow f$ and $g_{n}\downarrow g$. It follows from the Archimedean property that $f=g=:e$, and for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$ we have $e_{\alpha}-e\le g_{n}-f_{n}\le \frac{1}{n}h$, and similarly $e_{\alpha}-e\ge -\frac{1}{n}h$, thus justifying $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{ru}}e$.

Assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ satisfies the conditions of part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{todovs}. Let $Q,R$ be the corresponding controlling sets. Since $Q$ is upward directed and bounded from above, we may set $q_{0}:=\bigvee Q$. Similarly, we may set $r_{0}:=\bigwedge R$. Then, we have $r_{0}-q_{0}=\bigwedge\left(R-Q\right)=0_{E}$, and so $q_{0}=r_{0}=:e$. It then follows from Proposition~\ref{do} that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} e$.

(ii): By part~(iv) of Proposition~\ref{oca} every monotone order bounded net is order Cauchy, hence order convergent, thus has an extremum.

Assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ is directed order Cauchy, so that $e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} 0_{E}$. Since $\mathrm{do}\ge\mathrm{o}$, we have $e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, and as $E$ is complete with respect to order convergence, there is $e\in E$ such that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$. There is $P\downarrow 0_{E}$ which witnesses $e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} 0_{E}$. That is, for every $p\in P$ there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $-p\le e_{\alpha}-e_{\beta}\le p$, for every $\alpha,\beta\ge\alpha_{0}$. Taking the order limit in the second variable yields $-p\le e_{\alpha}-e\le p$, for every $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$. Thus, $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} e$, and so $E$ is directed order complete.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{monodo}
Recall that $\ell_{1}^{*}=\ell_{\8}$, and so we may view $\ell_{1}$ isometrically embedded into $\ell_{\8}\left(X\right)$, where $X:=\mathrm{B}_{\ell_{\8}}$. Let $E:=\left\{\left(e,f\right)\in \ell_{\8}\left(X\right)^{2}: e-f\in\ell_{1}\right\}$. We claim that $E$ is monotone complete, but not complete with respect to directed order convergence. To show the former let $P\subseteq E_{+}$ be directed and such that $P\le \left(e_{0},f_{0}\right)\in E$. For every $p\in P$ we have $p=\left(e_{p},f_{p}\right)$, where $\0\le e_{p}\le e_{0}$, $\0\le f_{p}\le f_{0}$ and $g_{p}:=e_{p}-f_{p}\in\ell_{1}$.

Let us show that $\left(g_{p}\right)_{p\in P}$ is norm Cauchy in $\ell_{1}$. If this is not the case, there are $\varepsilon>0$ and an increasing sequence $\left(p_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq P$ such that $\left\|g_{p_{n+1}}-g_{p_{n}}\right\|\ge\varepsilon$. However, for every $x\in X$ we have that $\left(e_{p}\left(x\right)\right)_{p\in P}$ and $\left(f_{p}\left(x\right)\right)_{p\in P}$ are increasing nets bounded in $\mathbb{R}$. Hence, $\left(e_{p_{n}}\left(x\right)\right)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ and $\left(f_{p_{n}}\left(x\right)\right)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ are increasing bounded sequences in $\mathbb{R}$, and so they converge. It follows that $\left(g_{p_{n}}\left(x\right)\right)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ also converges, and so $g_{p_{n+1}}\left(x\right)-g_{p_{n}}\left(x\right)\to 0$, for every $x\in X$. Since $X=\mathrm{B}_{\ell_{\8}}$, we conclude that $g_{p_{n+1}}-g_{p_{n}}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{w}} \0$ in $\ell_1$, which by Schur's theorem implies $g_{p_{n+1}}-g_{p_{n}}\to \0$, contradicting $\left\|g_{p_{n+1}}-g_{p_{n}}\right\|\ge\varepsilon$.

It follows that there is $g\in \ell_{1}$ such that $g_{p}\to g$ in norm, hence $g_{p}\left(x\right)\to g\left(x\right)$, for every $x\in X$. We also have that for every $x\in X$ there are $e\left(x\right)\le e_{0}\left(x\right)$ and $f\left(x\right)\le f_{0}\left(x\right)$ such that $e_{p}\left(x\right)\uparrow e\left(x\right)$ and $f_{p}\left(x\right)\uparrow f\left(x\right)$. We can now conclude that $e,f\in \ell_{\8}\left(X\right)$, $\left(e,f\right)=\bigvee P$ in $\ell_{\8}\left(X\right)^{2}$, and $e-f=g\in\ell_{1}$. Hence, $\left(e,f\right)\in E$ and $\left(e,f\right)=\bigvee P$ in $E$.

Let us now prove that $E$ is not directed order complete. Since $\ell_{1}$ is not reflexive, there are $g\in \ell_{1}^{**}\setminus \ell_{1}$ and a net $\left(g_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq\mathrm{B}_{\ell_{1}}$ which $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-converges to $g$ in $\ell_{1}^{**}$. Viewing $\ell_{1}^{**}$ as isometrically embedded into $\ell_{\8}\left(X\right)$, we have that $g_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\to g\left(x\right)$, for every $x\in X$.

For every $\alpha$ and $x\in X$ put $h_{\alpha}\left(x\right):=\bigvee_{\beta,\gamma\ge\alpha}\left|g_{\beta}\left(x\right)-g_{\gamma}\left(x\right)\right|\le 2$. Then, $h_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\downarrow\0$, for every $x\in X$, and so $f_{\alpha}:=\left(h_{\alpha},h_{\alpha}\right)\downarrow\left(\0,\0\right)$ in $E$. For every $\alpha$ let $e_{\alpha}:=\left(g_{\alpha},\0\right)$; for every $\beta,\gamma\ge\alpha$ we have $-f_{\alpha}\le e_{\beta}-e_{\gamma}\le f_{\alpha}$. We conclude that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is directed order Cauchy.

Assume that there is $e\in E$ with $e=\left(u,v\right)$ such that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} e$. For every $\beta\ge \alpha$ taking the limit in $-f_{\alpha}\le e_{\beta}-e_{\gamma}\le f_{\alpha}$ with respect to $\gamma$ yields $-f_{\alpha}\le e_{\beta}-e\le f_{\alpha}$. In particular, for every $\alpha$ and $x\in X$ we have $\left|v\left(x\right)\right|\le h_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\downarrow 0$ and $\left|g_{\alpha}\left(x\right)-u\left(x\right)\right|\le h_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\downarrow 0$, thus $v=\0$ and $g_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\to u\left(x\right)$, for every $x\in X$. We conclude that $g=u=u-v\in\ell_{1}$, contradiction.
\qed
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{ocl}Let $E$ be an ordered vector space.
\item[(i)] Order convergence and directed order convergence in $E$ are convergence structures, which are Hausdorff, meaning that convergent nets have unique limits.
\item[(ii)] Order convergence is linear if and only if directed order convergence is linear if and only if $E$ is directed and Archimedean.
\item[(iii)] If $E$ is directed and Archimedean, relative uniform convergence is a linear Hausdorff convergence structure. Moreover, boundednesses with respect to order, directed order and relative uniform convergences are equivalent to order boundedness.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We only treat order convergence. The case of directed order convergence is similar.

(i): It is clear that a constant net order converges to its value, and that a quasi-subnet of an order convergent net order converges to the same limit. Assume that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$, $f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$, and $g_{\alpha}\in\left\{e_{\alpha},f_{\alpha}\right\}$, for every $\alpha$. It follows from part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{ocv} that $e_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$. Let $P$ be as in part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{ocv} for $\left(e_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$. For every $\alpha$ we have that $g_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}\in\left\{e_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}, 0_{E}\right\}$, and so it is easy to see that $P$ witnesses $g_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$. Using part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{ocv} again we conclude that $g_{\alpha}=g_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha}+f_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}+e=e$. Hausdorffness follows immediately from Proposition~\ref{oc}.

(ii): Necessity: The fact that $E$ is Archimedean is proved similarly to the implication (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) in Proposition~\ref{oca}. Let $e\in E$; it follows from linearity of order convergence that $\frac{1}{n}e\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, witnessed by $P\subseteq E_{+}$ with $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$. It follows that there are $0_{E}\le p\in P$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\frac{1}{n}e\le p$. Then, $np\ge e,0_{E}$, showing that $E$ is directed.

Sufficiency: In the light of part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{ocv}, we only need to prove that if $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} e$ and $\mathbb{R}\ni r_{\alpha}\to r$, then $r_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} re$. It is easy to see that $re_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} re$, and so without loss of generality we may assume that $r=0$. By passing to a tail, we may also assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq\left[-u,u\right]$, for $u\in E_{+}$. Then, $r_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{ru}} 0_{E}$ with regulator $u$, which implies $r_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, according to Proposition~\ref{oca}.

The case of directed order convergence is analogous.

(iii): The fact that $\mathrm{ru}$ is a linear convergence structure is proven in \cite[Section~10]{btw} (note that it is immaterial for that result whether $E$ is a lattice).

Assume that $B\subseteq\left[-u,u\right]$, for $u\in E_{+}$. Let $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq B$ and let $\left(r_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ converge to $0$. Arguing as in the previous step, we see that $r_{\alpha}e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$. We conclude that $E$ is bounded with respect to order convergence. The converse follows from the fact that order convergence is locally order bounded and \cite[Corollary~8.3]{bctv} (note that it is immaterial for that result whether $E$ is a lattice).
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{do=ru}
Let $E$ be an ordered Banach space such that the norm induces a locally full convergence\footnote{This condition is usually described as ``$E$ has a normal cone'', see \cite[Theorem~2.23]{at}.} such that every net which decreases to $0_{E}$ converges in norm (to $0_{E}$). Then, $\mathrm{ru}=\mathrm{do}\ge\|\cdot\|$ on $E$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
First, as an ordered Banach space, $E$ is Archimedean (see \cite[Lemma~2.3]{at}), and so $\mathrm{ru}\ge \mathrm{do}$, by Proposition~\ref{oca}. Since the norm convergence is locally full and every net which decreases to $0_{E}$ converges in norm to $0_{E}$, it follows from the comment above that $\mathrm{do}\ge\|\cdot\|$ on $E$.

Assume that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} 0_{E}$, witnessed by $P\downarrow 0_{E}$. Then, $P\to 0_{E}$ in norm, and so there are $h\in E_{+}$ and $\left(p_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq P$ such that $p_{n}\le\frac{1}{n}h$ (the proof of \cite[Lemma~1.1]{tt} goes through, since the elements of the net are positive). For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $\alpha_{n}$ such that $-\frac{1}{n}h\le -p_{n}\le e_{\alpha} \le p_{n}\le \frac{1}{n}h$, whenever $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$. We conclude that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{ru}} 0_{E}$ with regulator $h$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{jochen}
Consider the ordered Banach space $F$ presented in \cite[Example~2.6]{glu}, which has an order unit (hence directed), and satisfies the condition of Proposition~\ref{do=ru}, but contains an increasing order bounded sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq F$ which is not norm-Cauchy. Then, this sequence is not $\mathrm{do}$-Cauchy, since otherwise it would follow that $f_{n}-f_{m}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} 0_{F}$, and hence $f_{n}-f_{m}\to 0_{F}$, and it does not have a supremum, because $f_{n}\uparrow f$ would imply $f_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} f$, and hence $f_{n}\to f$.
\qed
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{pervdense}
If $F$ is an Archimedean vector lattice and $E\subseteq F$ is an order dense subspace, then $f=\bigvee\left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}$, for every $f\in F_{+}$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
As $F$ is a lattice, it is enough to show that $f$ is a minimal upper bound for $\left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}$. Assume that there is $f>g\ge\left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}$. Then, there is $h\in \left(0_{F},f-g\right]\cap E$, but then $\left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}+h\subseteq\left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}$ and part~(i) of Lemma~\ref{arch} yields that $h=0_{F}$, contradiction.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{odm}
If $F$ is an Archimedean vector lattice and $E\subseteq F$ is an order dense majorizing subspace, then $E$ is supremum-dense in $F$. In particular, the embedding of $E$ into $F$ preserves arbitrary infima and suprema.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
For $f\in F$ find $e\in E$ with $e\ge f$. Then, $e-f=\bigvee \left[0_{F},e-f\right]_{E}$, hence
\[f=e-\bigvee\left[0_{F},e-f\right]_{E}=\bigwedge\left[f,e\right]_{E},\]
which implies $f=\bigwedge \left[f\right)_{E}$. Thus, $E$ is infimum-dense in $F$, which is equivalent to being supremum-dense. The last claim follows from Proposition~\ref{ocp}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{pervdir}
Let $F$ be an Archimedean vector lattice and let $E\subseteq F$ be an order dense subspace. Let $P\subseteq F_{+}$ be upward directed and let $g\in F$ be such that $g=\bigvee P$. Then there is an upward directed $Q\subseteq \bigcup_{p\in P}\left[0_{F},p\right]_{E}$ such that $g=\bigvee Q$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The family of all nonempty directed subsets of $R:=\bigcup_{p\in P}\left[0_{F},p\right]_{E}$ is nonempty (as it contains $\left\{0_{F}\right\}$) and every chain of such subsets has an upper bound (its union). By Zorn's lemma there is a maximal member $Q$ of this family. We will show that $g=\bigvee Q$. Assume that this is false, and so there is $f\in F$ with $Q\le f< g$. Since $g=\bigvee P$, we can find $P\ni g_{1}\not\le f$. As $E$ is order dense in $F$, there is $e\in E\cap \left(0_{F},\left(g_{1}-f\right)^{+}\right]$.

For a fixed $h\in Q$ let us show that $h+e\in R$. There is $g_{2}\in P$ such that $h\in \left[0_{F},g_{2}\right]$. Since $P$ is directed, it contains $g_{3}\ge g_{1},g_{2}$. Then, $h\le g_{2}\le g_{3}$ and $h\in Q\le f$ yield $h\le g_{3}\wedge f$. Hence,
\[h+e\le g_{3}\wedge f+\left(g_{1}-f\right)^{+}\le g_{3}\wedge f+\left(g_{3}-f\right)^{+}=g_{3},\]
and so $h+e\in \left[0_{F},g_{3}\right]_{E}\subseteq R$.

It follows that $Q\cup \left(Q+e\right)\subseteq R$. Furthermore, $Q\cup \left(Q+e\right)$ is directed: if $h_{1}\in Q$ and $h_{2}\in Q+e$, find $Q\ni h_{3}\ge h_{1},h_{2}-e$; then $h_{3}+e\ge h_{1},h_{2}$ (other cases are obvious). Due to maximality of $Q$, we have $Q+e\subseteq Q$. As $Q$ is bounded from above and $F$ is Archimedean, $e\le 0_{F}$ by virtue of Lemma~\ref{arch}, contradicting the assumption on $e$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{pervdird}
Let $F$ be an Archimedean vector lattice and let $E\subseteq F$ be an order dense subspace. Let $P\subseteq F_{+}$ be directed downward with $\bigwedge P=0_{F}$ such that there are $p_{0}\in P$ and $e_{0}\in E$ with $p_{0}\le e_{0}$. Then, there is $Q\subseteq \left[0_{F},e_{0}\right]_{E}\cap \left(P+F_{+}\right)$ which is directed downward and such that $\bigwedge Q=0_{F}$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By replacing $P$ with $\left[0_{F},p_{0}\right]\cap P$ if needed, we may assume that $P\le p_{0}\le e_{0}$. Let $R:=e_{0}-P$, which is upward directed and satisfies $e_{0}=\bigvee R$. According to Proposition~\ref{pervdir}, there is an upward directed $S\subseteq \bigcup_{r\in R}\left[0_{F},r\right]_{E}$ such that $e_{0}=\bigvee S$. Finally, $Q:=e_{0}-S$ fulfills the requirements.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{pervasive}
For a directed Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is pervasive;
\item[(ii)] The image of $E$ under the natural embedding into $E^{\delta}$ is order dense;
\item[(iii)] For every $e\in E^{\delta}_{+}$ there is a directed $Q\subseteq E_{+}$ such that $e=\bigvee Q$;
\item[(iv)] For every $e<f$ we have that $\left[e,f\right]^{\partial}\simeq \left[e,f\right]_{E^{\delta}}$;
\item[(v)] $\left(E_{+}\right)^{\partial}\simeq\left(E^{\delta}\right)_{+}\cup \left\{+\8\right\}$, where if $E=\left\{0_{E}\right\}$ we set $+\8:=0_{E}$;
\item[(vi)] The embedding of $E_{+}$ into $E$ preserves arbitrary infima;
\item[(vii)] For every $P\subseteq E_{+}$ such that $\bigwedge_{E_{+}}P=0_{E}$ we have $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$;
\item[(viii)] For every $e\not\le 0_{E}$ there is $g>0_{E}$ such that $\left\{e,0_{E}\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{g\right\}^{\uparrow}$;
\item[(ix)] For every $e,f\in E_{+}$ with $e\not\le f$ there is $g>f$ such that $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{g\right\}^{\uparrow}$;
\item[(x)] For every $e,f$ with $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq E_{+}\setminus\left\{0_{E}\right\}$ there is $g>0_{E}$ such that $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{g\right\}^{\uparrow}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is trivial. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) follows from applying Proposition~\ref{pervdir} to $\left\{e\right\}$. (v)$\Rightarrow$(ii) follows from the fact that $E_{+}$ is supremum-dense in $\left(E_{+}\right)^{\partial}$.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iv): First, note that $\left[e,f\right]_{E^{\delta}}$ is a complete lattice, which contains $\left[e,f\right]$. Hence, in order to prove that $\left[e,f\right]^{\partial}\simeq \left[e,f\right]_{E^{\delta}}$ it is enough to show that $\left[e,f\right]$ is supremum- and infimum-dense in $\left[e,f\right]_{E^{\delta}}$. Since translations on ordered vector spaces are order isomorphisms, without loss of generality we may assume that $e=0_{E}$. Now the supremum density follows directly from Proposition~\ref{pervdense}, and the fact that being a supremum of a set in a poset implies being a supremum in its order interval. Infimum density can be reduced to the preceding argument by taking $f=0_{E}$ and using the fact that additive inversion is an order anti-isomorphism.

(iv)$\Rightarrow$(v): By the argument above we only need to prove that $E_{+}$ is supremum- and infimum-dense in $\left(E^{\delta}\right)_{+}\cup \left\{+\8\right\}$. For every $0_{E^{\delta}}<f\in E^{\delta}$ there is $e\in E$ such that $f<e$. By assumption, we have
\[f=\bigvee_{\left[0_{E^{\delta}},e\right]_{E^{\delta}}}\left(\left[0_{E},e\right]\cap\left[0_{E^{\delta}},f\right]_{E^{\delta}}\right)=\bigvee_{\left[0_{E^{\delta}},e\right]_{E^{\delta}}}\left(E\cap\left[0_{E^{\delta}},f\right]_{E^{\delta}}\right).\] It is easy to see that then $f=\bigvee_{E^{\delta}}\left(E\cap\left[0_{E^{\delta}},f\right]_{E^{\delta}}\right)$. This argument shows supremum density; infimum density follows from the fact that $E$ is infimum-dense in $E^{\delta}$.

(v)$\Rightarrow$(vi): Assume that $Q\subseteq E_{+}$ and $e\in E_{+}$ are such that $e=\bigwedge_{E_{+}}Q$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{ocp}, it follows that $e=\bigwedge_{\left(E_{+}\right)^{\partial}}Q$, and it follows from the assumption that $e=\bigwedge_{\left(E^{\delta}\right)_{+}}Q$. As $E^{\delta}$ is a vector lattice, this implies that $e=\bigwedge_{E^{\delta}}Q$, and as all involved elements are in $E$, we conclude that $e=\bigwedge_{E}Q$.

(vi)$\Rightarrow$(vii) is trivial.

(vii)$\Rightarrow$(viii): If $e\not\le 0_{E}$, then $0_{E}$ is not the infimum of $\left\{e,0_{E}\right\}^{\uparrow}$ in $E$. By assumption it follows that $0_{E}$ is not the infimum of $\left\{e,0_{E}\right\}^{\uparrow}$ in $E_{+}$, and so there is a nonzero lower bound $g$ for this set in $E_{+}$. It is easy to see that this $g$ satisfies the requirements.

(viii)$\Rightarrow$(ii): For $0_{E^{\delta}}<h$, the set $Q:=\left(h-E^{\delta}_{+}\right)\cap E$ is a cut in $E$ which strictly contains $-E_{+}$, and so there is $e\in Q$ such that $e\not\le 0_{E^{\delta}}$. Take $0_{E^{\delta}}<g\in E$ such that $\left\{0_{E},e\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq g+E_{+}$, from where $g\in\left\{0_{E},e\right\}^{\uparrow\downarrow}\subseteq Q\subseteq h-E^{\delta}_{+}$, hence $g\in \left(0_{E^{\delta}},h\right]$.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(viii): Assume that $F$ is a vector lattice, and that $E\subseteq F$ is an order dense subspace. Take $E\ni e\not\le 0_{E}$. Then, $e^{+}>0_{F}$, and so we can find $g\in E\cap \left(0_{F},e^{+}\right]$. Now if $f\ge e,0_{E}$, then $f\ge e^{+}$, and so $f\ge g$, as required.

(viii)$\Rightarrow$(ix): Applying (viii) to $e-f$ we get $h>0_{E}$ such that $\left\{e-f,0_{E}\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{h\right\}^{\uparrow}$. Then, $g:=h+f$ satisfies the requirements.

(ix)$\Rightarrow$(viii): Since $E$ is directed, we have that $e=u-v$, where $u,v\in E_{+}$ with $u\not\le v$. Hence, by (ix) there is $w>v$ such that $\left\{u,v\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{w\right\}^{\uparrow}$. Then, $g:=w-v$ satisfies the requirements.

(x)$\Rightarrow$(viii) is obtained by taking $f=0_{E}$.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(x): As $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow}\subsetneq E_{+}$ it follows that $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow\downarrow}\supsetneq -E_{+}=0_{E^{\delta}}$, which means that $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow\downarrow}=e\vee_{E^{\delta}}f$ is a strictly positive element of $E^{\delta}$. By (ii) there is $g\in E$ such that $0_{E^{\delta}}<g\le e\vee_{E^{\delta}}f$. The latter means $g\in\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow\downarrow}$, which translates into $\left\{e,f\right\}^{\uparrow}\subseteq \left\{g\right\}^{\uparrow}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{pervint}
Analogously to (v)$\Rightarrow$(vi) one can show that in a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space embeddings of order intervals preserve arbitrary suprema and infima.
\qed
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{arch1}
If an ordered vector space $F$ contains a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ as a supremum-dense subspace, then $F$ is pervasive and $E$ is order dense and majorizing in $F$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
First, according to Proposition~\ref{arch0}, $F$ is Archimedean, and so $F^{\delta}$ exists. Moreover, $E$ is supremum-dense in $F^{\delta}$, therefore $F^{\delta}=E^{\delta}$. By Theorem~\ref{pervasive}, $E$ is order dense in $E^{\delta}$, and since we have $E\subseteq F\subseteq E^{\delta}$, it follows that $E$ is order dense in $F$. It also follows that $F$ is order dense in $F^{\delta}$, and so by Theorem~\ref{pervasive}, $F$ is pervasive.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{dedeperv}
If $E$ is a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space, then $E^{\delta}$ is the unique Dedekind complete vector lattice which contains $E$ as an order dense majorizing subspace.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{o=do}
If $E$ is a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space, then order convergence and directed order convergence agree on $E$.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We only need to show that order convergence is stronger than directed order convergence. In light of Proposition~\ref{oca}, it is enough to show that if $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ is (directed) order null in $E^{\delta}$, then it is directed order null in $E$. Let $P\subseteq E^{\delta}$ be a directed downward set which witnesses the order convergence of the net. According to Proposition~\ref{pervdird}, there is $Q\subseteq E\cap \left(P+E_{+}\right)$ which is directed downward and such that $\bigwedge Q=0_{E^{\delta}}$. For every $q\in Q$ there is $p\in P$ with $q\ge p$, and so there is $\alpha_{0}$ such that $\pm e_{\alpha}\le p\le q$, as soon as $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$. Hence, $Q$ witnesses $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} 0_{E}$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{wp}
For an ordered vector space $E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is a vector lattice;
\item[(ii)] For every $e\in E$ there are $f,g\in E_{+}$ such that $e=f-g$ and $f\wedge_{E}g=0_{E}$;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is weakly pervasive and for every $e\in E$ there are $f,g\in E_{+}$ such that $e=f-g$ and $f\wedge_{E_{+}}g=0_{E}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(iii): To prove that $E$ is weakly pervasive assume that $e,f\in E_{+}$ are such that $e\wedge_{E_{+}}f=0_{E}$. If $g\in E$ is such that $g\le e,f$, then $g^{+}\in E_{+}$ together with $g^{+}\le e,f$ yield $g^{+}=0_{E}$, hence $g\le 0_{E}$. Thus, $e\wedge_{E} f=0_{E}$.

For every $e\in E$ we have that $e^{+},e^{-}\in E_{+}$, $e=e^{+}-e^{-}$ and $e^{+}\wedge_{E_{+}}e^{-}=0_{E}$.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii) follows from the definition of weak pervasiveness.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): Let $e\in E$ and let $f,g\in E_{+}$ be such that $e=f-g$ and $f\wedge g=0_{E}$. Then, $e^{+}= \left(f-g\right)^{+}=f-f\wedge g=f$. Hence, every element of $E$ has a positive part, which is sufficient for $E$ to be a lattice.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{pervcomplete}
For a directed ordered vector space $E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is a Dedekind complete vector lattice;
\item[(ii)] $E$ is pervasive, Archimedean and complete with respect to order convergence;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is monotone complete and pervasive;
\item[(iv)] $E$ is directed, Archimedean, weakly pervasive, and such that every order bounded totally ordered set in $E$ has a supremum.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is established in \cite[Proposition~9.10]{btw}. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) follows from part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{monc}. In (iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv), Archimedeanness follows from part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{monc}, while the rest is straightforward. In (iv)$\Rightarrow$(i), the fact that $E$ is a lattice is proved in \cite[Theorem~4.12]{gluck}, while Dedekind completeness follows from \cite[Corollary~1]{markowsky}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{pervid}
Let $F$ be a vector lattice, let $E\subseteq F$ be an order dense subspace, and let $H\subseteq E$ be a directed full subspace. Then $H$ is an order dense majorizing subspace of $I_{F}\left(H\right)$.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
First, since $H$ is directed, it is easy to see that $I_{F}\left(H\right)=\bigcup_{h\in H_{+}}\left[-h,h\right]$. Let $0_{F}<f\in I_{F}\left(H\right)$, so that there is $h\in H_{+}$ with $f\le h$. As $E$ is order dense, there is $e\in\left(0_{F},f\right]\cap E$. In particular, $0_{F}\le e\le h$, and since $H$ is full we conclude that $e\in H$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{pervideal}
Let $E$ be a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space and let $H\subseteq E$ be a directed full subspace. Then:
\item[(i)] $H$ is pervasive and $I_{E^{\delta}}\left(H\right)=H^{\delta}$;
\item[(ii)] $\mathrm{o}_{E}$ and $\mathrm{o}_{H}$ agree on subsets of $H$ which are order bounded in $H$.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
(i) follows from Corollary~\ref{dedeperv} and Proposition~\ref{pervid}.

(ii): Let $h\in H_{+}$. It follows from (i) that $R:=\left[-h,h\right]_{H^{\delta}}$ is an order interval in $E^{\delta}$. Hence, the restrictions of both $\mathrm{o}_{E^{\delta}}$ and $\mathrm{o}_{H^{\delta}}$ to $R$ agree with $\mathrm{o}_{R}$ (see \cite[Lemma~2.2]{abt}). By the last part of Proposition~\ref{oca}, we have $\mathrm{o}_{E}=\left.\mathrm{o}_{E^{\delta}}\right|_{E}$ and $\mathrm{o}_{H}=\left.\mathrm{o}_{H^{\delta}}\right|_{H}$. Since $\left[-h,h\right]\subseteq R$, we conclude that $\left.\mathrm{o}_{E}\right|_{\left[-h,h\right]}=\left.\mathrm{o}_{E^{\delta}}\right|_{\left[-h,h\right]}=\left.\mathrm{o}_{H^{\delta}}\right|_{\left[-h,h\right]}=\left.\mathrm{o}_{H}\right|_{\left[-h,h\right]}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{nonperv}
We will denote $L_{\8}:=L_{\8}\left[0,1\right]$ and let
\[E:=\left\{\left(e,f\right)\in L_{\8}\times L_{\8}: \textstyle\int e = \int f\right\}.\]
First, let us prove that $E^{\delta}=L_{\8}\times L_{\8}$. It is enough to show that $E$ is supremum-dense in $L_{\8}\times L_{\8}$. Let $g,h\in L_{\8}$. If $\int g = \int h$, then $\left(g,h\right)\in E$. Alternatively, without loss of generality we may assume that $\delta:=\int g - \int h>0$. Let $g_{1}:=g-2\delta\1_{\left[0,1/2\right]}$ and $g_{2}:=g-2\delta\1_{\left[1/2,1\right]}$. We have that $\int g_{i}=\int g-\delta=\int h$, for $i=1,2$. Hence, $\left(g_{1},h\right), \left(g_{2},h\right)\in E$ and $\left(g_{1},h\right)\vee \left(g_{2},h\right)=\left(g,h\right)$.

To prove that $E$ is not pervasive, we use the condition (ii) in Theorem~\ref{pervasive}: we show that $E$ is not order dense in $E^{\delta}=L_{\8}\times L_{\8}$. Indeed, if $\left(e,f\right)\in E_{+}$ is such that $\left(e,f\right)\le \left(\1,\0\right)$, then $f=\0$, hence $\int e=\int f=0$, and so $e=\0$.

Let $H\subseteq E$ be full and directed. Let us show that $I_{E^{\delta}}\left(H\right)=H^{\delta}$, for which it is again enough to prove that $H$ is supremum-dense in $I_{E^{\delta}}\left(H\right)$. Let $\left(g,h\right)\in I_{E^{\delta}}\left(H\right)$, so that there is $\left(e,f\right)\in H_{+}$ with $\left|g\right|\le e$ and $\left|h\right|\le f$. If $f=\0$, then $\int e=\int f=0$, hence $e=\0$, and so $g=h=\0$, implying $\left(g,h\right)\in H$. Similarly, $e=\0$ also yields $\left(g,h\right)\in H$. We thus assume that $e,f>\0$. Also, we may again assume that $\delta:=\int g - \int h>0$.

There are disjoint measurable $A,B\subseteq\left[0,1\right]$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\lambda\left(A\right)=\lambda\left(B\right)=\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon\1_{A}, \varepsilon\1_{B}\le e$. It follows that for
\[g_{1}:=g-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\1_{A}\quad\text{and}\quad g_{2}:=g-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\1_{B}\]
we have $\int g_{1}=\int g_{2}=\int h$, and so $\left(g_{1},h\right),\left(g_{2},h\right)\in E$. Since $f\ge\0$ and $\varepsilon\1_{A}\le e$, we get
\[\left(e,f\right)\ge \left(g_{1},h\right)\ge -\left(e,f\right) - \frac{\delta}{\varepsilon^{2}}\left(e,f\right)=-\frac{\delta+\varepsilon^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\left(e,f\right),\]
implying $\left(g_{1},h\right)\in H$. Similarly, $\left(g_{2},h\right)\in H$, and moreover, disjointness of $A$ and $B$ yields $\left(g_{1},h\right)\vee \left(g_{2},h\right)=\left(g,h\right)$.
\qed
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{prepervasive}
Theorem~\ref{pervasive} remains partially valid for pre-Riesz spaces. Namely, the conditions (i), (vi), (vii), (viii) and (ix) are equivalent to the version of the condition (ii) in which $E^{\delta}$ is replaced with $E^{\rho}$. We only need to supply a new proof for (i)$\Rightarrow$(vi). Assume that $F$ is a vector lattice, and $E$ is order dense in $F$. Let $Q\subseteq E_{+}$ be such that $\bigwedge_{E_{+}}Q=0_{E}$, and let $e\in E$ be a lower bound for $Q$. Then, $e^{+}\in F$ is also a lower bound for $Q$. If $e\not\le 0_{E}$, then $e^{+}>0_{F}$, and since $E$ is order dense in $F$, there is $0_{E}<g\in E$ such that $g\le e^{+}\le Q$, which contradicts $\bigwedge_{E_{+}}Q=0_{E}$. Thus, $\bigwedge_{E}Q=0_{E}$.

It follows that a pervasive pre-Riesz space is Archimedean whenever
\[\bigwedge\nolimits_{E_{+}}\left\{\tfrac{1}{n}f: n\in\mathbb{N}\right\}=0_{E},\quad\text{for every }f\in E_{+}.\] In particular, every pervasive almost Archimedean (see \cite[Section~1.2, Exercise~6]{at}) pre-Riesz space is Archimedean.
\qed
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{l:vector lattice totally ordered disjointness free}
   Let $E$ be a pre-Riesz space. The following conditions are equivalent:
    \item[(i)] $E$ is totally ordered;
    \item[(ii)] $E$ is a disjointness-free lattice;
    \item[(iii)] $E$ is disjointness-free and pervasive.\medskip

    If in this case $E$ is also Archimedean, then $\dim E\le 1$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Clearly, $E$ is a lattice. Moreover, since the infimum of two elements is their minimum, it follows that $E$ is disjointness-free.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): If $E$ is not totally ordered, then after translation there is an element $e$ incomparable with $0_{E}$, and so $e^{+}$ and $e^{-}$ are nonzero disjoint elements.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is trivial.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i): First, we show that $E^{\rho}$ is disjointness-free. Indeed, if $0_{E^{\rho}}<g,h\in E^{\rho}_{+}$ are disjoint, according to Remark~\ref{prepervasive}, there are $e\in\left(0_{E^{\rho}},g\right]\cap E$ and $f\in\left(0_{E^{\rho}},h\right]\cap E$, which are then also disjoint, contradiction. Now we can apply the equivalence of (i) and (ii) to $E^{\rho}$ and conclude that it is totally ordered. Therefore every two elements in $E^{\rho}$, and hence in $E$, are comparable.

It is well-known (see \cite[Chapter~1, Exercise~14]{ab0}) that an Archimedean totally ordered vector space is $\{0\}$ or $\mathbb{R}$, showing the final statement.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{pervatom}
Let $F$ be an Archimedean vector lattice, and let $E\subseteq F$ be an order dense subspace. Then, $f\in F_{+}$ is an atom in $F$ if and only if $f\in E$ and it is an atom in $E$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Necessity: There is $e\in \left(0_{F},f\right]\cap E\subseteq\mathbb{R} f\cap E$, and so there is $r>0$ such that $rf\in E$. Thus, $f\in E$, and clearly it is an atom there.

Sufficiency: Assume that $f$ is not an atom in $F$, so that there are disjoint $g,h\in\left(0_{F},f\right]$. Find $u\in \left(0_{F},g\right]\cap E$ and $v\in \left(0_{F},h\right]\cap E$. It follows that $u,v\in \left[0_{F},f\right]_{E}$ are linearly independent, contradicting the fact that $f$ is an atom in $E$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{pervatomic}
Let $F$ be an Archimedean vector lattice, and let $E\subseteq F$ be an order dense subspace. Then $F$ is atomic if and only if $E$ is atomic. In particular, in this case every element of $E_{+}$ is the supremum of a collection of atoms.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Necessity: Every element of $F_{+}$ is a supremum of a collection of atoms in $F$. According to Proposition~\ref{pervatom}, atoms in $F$ are also atoms in $E$, and so every element of $E_{+}$ is a supremum in $F$ (hence in $E$) of a collection of atoms in $E$.

Sufficiency: Let $f>0_{F}$. There is $e\in\left(0_{F},f\right]\cap E$, and since $E$ is atomic, there is an atom $g\in\left(0_{F},e\right]\cap E$. Then, $0_{F}<g\le f$, and according to Proposition~\ref{pervatom}, $g$ is an atom in $F$. As $f$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $F$ is atomic.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
An extension of Corollary~\ref{pervatomic} and more information about atoms in pervasive spaces can be found in \cite{mz}.
\qed
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{pervurisohn}
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff space and let $E\subseteq \mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ be an order dense subspace and let $U_{1},\dots,U_{n}\subseteq K$ be nonempty open sets. Then, there is $f\in \left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which vanishes outside of $U_{1}\cup\dots\cup U_{n}$ and such that $f^{-1}\left(1\right)\cap U_{k}\ne\varnothing$, for every $k=1,\dots,n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
First, assume that $U_{1},\dots,U_{n}$ are disjoint and fix $k=1,\dots,n$. By Urysohn's lemma there is $f_{k}\in \mathcal{C}\left(K\right)\cap \left(\0,\1_{U_{k}}\right]$. Since $E$ is order dense in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$, we can find some $e_{k}\in\left(\0,f_{k}\right]\cap E$. In particular, $e_{k}$ vanishes outside of $U_{k}$, and so it attains its norm at some point $x_{k}\in U_{k}$. Then, $f:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\|e_{k}\|}e_{k}\in \left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ vanishes outside of $U_{1}\cup\dots\cup U_{n}$, and moreover $f\left(x_{k}\right)=1$ for every $k=1,\dots,n$.

In the general case, we first find disjoint nonempty open sets $V_{1},\dots,V_{m}$ such that $V_{1}\cup\dots\cup V_{m}\subseteq U_{1}\cup\dots\cup U_{n}$ and for every $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ there is $l\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ so that $V_{l}\subseteq U_{k}$. Their existence can be proved by induction over $n$.

The case $n=1$ is trivial. If the claim is proved for $n$, and $U_{0},\dots,U_{n}$ are open and nonempty, by the induction hypothesis we can find $V_{1},\dots,V_{m}$ corresponding to $U_{1},\dots,U_{n}$. Let us show that the collection of all nonempty sets among $V_{i}\cap U_{0}$, $V_{i}\setminus \overline{U_{0}}$, $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, and $U_{0}\setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\overline{V_{i}}$ satisfies the requirements. For $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ find $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ such that $V_{i}\subseteq U_{j}$. Then, one of $V_{i}\cap U_{0}$, $V_{i}\setminus \overline{U_{0}}$ is nonempty and contained in $V_{i}$, hence in $U_{j}$. Also, either $V_{i}\cap U_{0}\ne\varnothing$, for some $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, or $U_{0}\setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\overline{V_{i}}$ is nonempty and contained in $U_{0}$. This verifies the conclusion of the induction step.

Now, according to the special case, there is $f\in \left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which vanishes outside of $V_{1}\cup\dots\cup V_{m}\subseteq U_{1}\cup\dots\cup U_{n}$ and such that $f^{-1}\left(1\right)\cap V_{l}\ne\varnothing$, for every $l\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. For every $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ find $l$ as above; it follows that $f^{-1}\left(1\right)\cap U_{k}\supseteq f^{-1}\left(1\right)\cap V_{l}\ne\varnothing$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{pervnoc}
Let $E\subseteq \mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ be an order dense subspace, where $K$ is a compact Hausdorff space without isolated points. Then there is a net in $\left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which has no order Cauchy (in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$) subnets.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
There is a dense $Z\subseteq K$ such that $K\setminus Z$ is also dense (see \cite{hewitt}). Let $\mathcal{Z}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be the collections of all finite subsets of $Z$ and $K\setminus Z$, respectively, ordered by inclusion. For $z\in Z$ let $\mathcal{U}_{z}$ be the collection of all neighborhoods of $z$, ordered by reverse inclusion. Let $\Gamma:=\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{Y}\times \prod_{z\in Z}\mathcal{U}_{z}$, which is a directed set. Let $\gamma=\left(A,B,\left(U_{z}\right)_{z\in Z}\right)\in\Gamma$, where $A=\left\{z_{1},\dots,z_{n}\right\}\subseteq Z$. For every $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ we have that $V_{k}:=U_{z_{k}}\setminus B$ is a neighborhood of $z_{k}$. Applying Lemma~\ref{pervurisohn} to $V_{1},\dots,V_{n}$, there is $f_{\gamma}\in \left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which vanishes on $B$ and such that $f^{-1}_{\gamma}\left(1\right)\cap V_{k}\ne\varnothing$, for every $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$.

Let $\left(f_{\gamma_{\delta}}\right)_{\delta\in\Delta}$ be a subnet of $\left(f_{\gamma}\right)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$. We claim that for every $\delta_{0}\in\Delta$ we have $\bigvee_{\delta\ge\delta_{0}}f_{\gamma_{\delta}}=\1$ and $\bigwedge_{\delta\ge\delta_{0}}f_{\gamma_{\delta}}=\0$. Once this is established, it will follow immediately from Proposition~\ref{ocauchy} that $\left(f_{\gamma_{\delta}}\right)_{\delta\in\Delta}$ is not order Cauchy.

For the former claim, let $U\ne\varnothing$ be an open set. As $Z$ is dense, we can find $x\in Z\cap U$. There is $\delta\ge\delta_{0}$ such that $\gamma_{\delta}\ge\left(\left\{x\right\},\varnothing, \left(U_{z}\right)_{z\in Z}\right)$, where $U_{x}:=U$ and $U_{z}:=K$ if $z\ne x$. Then, $\gamma_{\delta}=\left(A,B,\left(V_{z}\right)_{z\in Z}\right)$, where $x\in A$ and $V_{x}\subseteq U_{x}=U$. We have that
\[f^{-1}_{\gamma_{\delta}}\left(1\right)\cap U\supseteq f^{-1}_{\gamma_{\delta}}\left(1\right)\cap V_{x}\ne\varnothing.\] Since $U$ was chosen arbitrarily, it follows from \cite[Lemma~3.1]{bt} that $\bigvee_{\delta\ge\delta_{0}}f_{\gamma_{\delta}}=\1$.

We now prove the latter claim. For every $y\in K\setminus Z$, there is $\delta\ge\delta_{0}$ such that $\gamma_{\delta}\ge\left(\varnothing,\left\{y\right\},\left(K\right)_{z\in Z}\right)$. Arguing as in the previous step, we see that $f_{\gamma_{\delta}}\left(y\right)=0$, and since $y$ was arbitrary, it is easy to conclude that $\bigwedge_{\delta\ge\delta_{0}}f_{\gamma_{\delta}}=\0$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{ordprec}
For a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is order locally pre-compact;
\item[(ii)] All order intervals are order pre-compact;
\item[(iii)] Order convergence is topological on the intervals in $E$;
\item[(iv)] Order convergence has the \emph{Choquet property}, i.e.\ if $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is not order-null, it has a subnet which has no further order-null subnets;
\item[(v)] $E$ is atomic;
\item[(vi)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$.\medskip

Moreover, on order bounded subsets of $E$ order convergence agrees with pointwise convergence.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Fix $e\in E_{+}$, and let $\Gamma:=\mathbb{N}\times\left[0_{E},e\right]$, ordered by the first component. Define a net $\left(e_{\gamma}\right)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ by $e_{\left(n,f\right)}:=\frac{1}{n}f$. The tails of this net are of the form $\left[0_{E},\frac{1}{n}e\right]$, for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$. It follows that $e_{\gamma}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{ru}} 0_{E}$, therefore $e_{\gamma}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, and so there is $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\left[0_{E},\frac{1}{n}e\right]$ is order pre-compact. It is easy to deduce from this that every order interval in $E$ is order pre-compact.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) follows from the fact that every order convergent net is eventually order bounded, hence contained in an interval, which is order pre-compact.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv): Suppose that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is not order-null. If it is not eventually order bounded, it has a subnet with no further order bounded subnets (see \cite[Proposition~9.5]{bctv}; take into account the comment after \cite[Proposition~9.1]{bctv}). In particular, this subnet has no further order-null subnets.

If $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is eventually order bounded, without loss of generality we may assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq \left[-e,e\right]$, for some $e\in E_{+}$. By assumption, there is a topology $\tau$ on $\left[-e,e\right]$ which agrees with order convergence. As the net is not order-null, there are a $\tau$-neighborhood $U$ of $0_{E}$ and a majorizing $A'\subseteq A$ such that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A'}\subseteq \left[-e,e\right]\setminus U$. It is clear that no further subnet of $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A'}$ is order-null.

(ii),(iv)$\Rightarrow$(v): Assume that $e>0_{E}$ is such that $\left[0_{E},e\right]$ contains no atoms. The subspace $H:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[-ne,ne\right]$ satisfies the conditions of Corollary~\ref{pervideal}. Hence, without loss of generality we may assume that $E=H$, and so $e$ is an order unit in $E$. Furthermore, it remains an order unit in $E^{\delta}$, which we therefore may assume to be isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$, for some compact Hausdorff $K$ (see \cite[Theorem~45.4]{lz}). Thus, $E$ embeds as an order dense subspace of $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ and $e=\1$. By virtue of Proposition~\ref{oca}, order convergence in $E$ is the restriction of order convergence in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$. According to Proposition~\ref{pervatom}, $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ is atomless, and so $K$ has no isolated points (see \cite[Lemma~3.2]{abt}).

By Proposition~\ref{pervnoc} there is a net in $\left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which has no order Cauchy subnets. We conclude that $\left[0_{E},e\right]$ is not order pre-compact. This establishes (ii)$\Rightarrow$(v).

To prove (iv)$\Rightarrow$(v), we first adapt \cite[Lemma~9.12]{bctv} to order dense subspaces of $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$. To that end, we construct $f_{\alpha}$ as in the proof of that lemma, except that instead of requiring $f_{\alpha}\left(t_{\alpha}\right)=1$ we only demand that $f_{\alpha}^{-1}\left(1\right)\cap U_{t_{\alpha}}^{\alpha}\ne\varnothing$ (which we can achieve by Lemma~\ref{pervurisohn}).

Now, according to this modified result, there is a net in $\left[\0,\1\right]_{E}$ which is not order-null but such that its every subnet contains a further order-null subnet. This shows that order convergence does not have the Choquet property.

(v)$\Rightarrow$(vi): It follows from Corollary~\ref{pervatomic} that $E^{\delta}$ is atomic, and so isomorphic to an order dense ideal in $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ for some set $X$ (see \cite[Theorems~1.40 and~1.78]{ab0}). As $E$ is order dense in $E^{\delta}$, it is order dense in $\mathbb{R}^{X}$, and so contains all atoms of the latter, in particular, $\1_{\left\{x\right\}}$ for every $x\in X$.

(vi)$\Rightarrow$(ii),(iii): First, let $F$ be the ideal generated by $E$ in $\mathbb{R}^{X}$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{pervid}, $E$ is order dense and majorizing, hence supremum-dense in $F$, and so by Proposition~\ref{ocp}, order convergence in $E$ is the restriction of order convergence in $F$. Now, by \cite[Proposition~2.5]{abt}, order convergence in order bounded sets in $F$ agrees with the pointwise convergence, which is topological, and these sets are order pre-compact.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{automaticlat}
For a pervasive Archimedean ordered vector space $E$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is order locally compact;
\item[(ii)] Every order interval in $E$ is order compact;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice;
\item[(iv)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as an ideal of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) is proved analogously to the corresponding equivalence in Theorem~\ref{ordprec}. It is easy to see that order compactness of order intervals implies monotone completeness, and so in this case $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice, by virtue of Proposition~\ref{pervcomplete} and Theorem~\ref{ordprec}. Hence, we get (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii), while (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii) were already proven in \cite{abt}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{ordco}
If $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice, then every order continuous function on order intervals in $E$ is bounded and order uniformly continuous.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{automaticlat} and Theorem~\ref{ordprec}, the order intervals in $E$ are order compact, and order convergence in these intervals is induced by a linear topology. Hence, we may apply the properties of compact uniform spaces to order convergence in this case, and derive both claims.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
If $E$ is an order continuous Banach lattice, then the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is atomic;
\item[(ii)] For every $e\in E_{+}$, every order continuous real-valued function on $\left[0_{E},e\right]$ is bounded;
\item[(iii)] For every $e\in E_{+}$, every order continuous real-valued function on $\left[0_{E},e\right]$ is order uniformly continuous.
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Recall that order continuous Banach lattices are Dedekind complete (see \cite[Theorem~3.24]{ab0}), and so (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii),(iii) follow from Corollary~\ref{ordco}.

Let us show that order (uniform) continuity is equivalent to norm (uniform) continuity. Clearly, since order convergence is stronger than norm convergence, norm (uniform) continuity implies order (uniform) continuity. To prove the converse, assume that $\varphi\colon\left[0_{E},e\right]\to \mathbb{R}$ is uniformly order continuous, but not uniformly norm continuous. Then, there are $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $\left[0_{E},e\right]$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $e_{n}-f_{n}\to 0_{E}$ in norm, but $\left|\varphi\left(e_{n}\right)-\varphi\left(f_{n}\right)\right|\ge\varepsilon$, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. There is a subsequence $\left(n_{m}\right)_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that $e_{n_{m}}-f_{n_{m}}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$ (see \cite[Lemma~1.1]{tt}), which contradicts order uniform continuity, since $\left|\varphi\left(e_{n_{m}}\right)-\varphi\left(f_{n_{m}}\right)\right|\ge\varepsilon$, for every $m\in\mathbb{N}$. The ``non-uniform'' case is done analogously.

Now the condition (ii) is equivalent to boundedness of every norm continuous function on $\left[0_{E},e\right]$, for every $e\in E_{+}$. This condition is equivalent to compactness of $\left[0_{E},e\right]$, for every $e\in E_{+}$, which is further equivalent to atomicity of $E$ (see \cite[Theorem~1]{lipecky}). Hence, we get (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

Finally, the condition (iii) is equivalent to uniform norm continuity of every norm continuous function on $\left[0_{E},e\right]$, for every $e\in E_{+}$. It is easy to see that every uniformly norm continuous function on a convex norm bounded set is bounded. Hence, we get (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii).
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ordconst}
Let us show that order continuous functions on order intervals in $\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]$ are constant. Note that this is well known for linear functionals (see e.g.\ \cite[Exercise~1.25]{ab0}). Let $g\in \mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]_{+}$ and let $\varphi\colon\left[\0,g\right]\to\mathbb{R}$ be order continuous. Assume that $\0<h\le g$ is such that $\varphi\left(h\right)\ne \varphi\left(\0\right)$. Without loss of generality we may assume that $\varphi\left(\0\right)=0$ and $\varphi\left(h\right)=1$. Then, $U:=\varphi^{-1}\left(-\8,\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is an order open neighborhood of $\0$ in $[\0, g]$. Arguing as in the proof of \cite[Example~10.7]{btw} (but multiplying all the involved functions by $h$), we construct a dense $X\subseteq \left[0,1\right]$ and an increasing sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq U$ such that $f_{n}\left(x\right)\to h\left(x\right)$, for every $x\in X$. It follows that $f_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} h$, hence by order continuity we get $\frac{1}{2}>\varphi\left(f_{n}\right)\to \varphi\left(h\right)=1$, contradiction.
\qed
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{poly}
Let $K:=\left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\cup\left\{0\right\}$. Then, $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)\simeq c$ is an atomic vector lattice. Let $E$ be the space of the restrictions of polynomials to $K$. Since $E$ is norm dense in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$, for every $f\in \mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $e\in E$ such that $\|f-e\|\le\varepsilon$, hence $f-2\varepsilon\1\le e - \varepsilon \1 \le f$. This clearly implies that $E$ is supremum-dense in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$.

Next, we prove that $E$ has no atoms. Let $\0\ne e\in E_{+}$ and let $f\colon K\to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f\left(t\right):=te\left(t\right)$. Then, $f\in \left[\0,e\right]$. Assume that $f=re$, for some $r\in \mathbb{R}$. Then, for every $t\in K$ with $t\ne r$ we have $te\left(t\right)=re\left(t\right)$, hence $e\left(t\right)=0$. Therefore, $e$ has infinitely many zeros, which is impossible for a nonzero polynomial.

Let us show that bounded pointwise convergence on $\left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$ implies directed order convergence in $E$. Note that since order intervals in $E$ are pointwise pre-compact (as subsets of order intervals in the atomic vector lattice), this proves that they are also directed order pre-compact. Let $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E\cap\left[\0,\1\right]$ be pointwise null on $\left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$. For each $n\in \mathbb{N}$ let $q_{n} = 2\left(1-\frac{t}{2}\right)^{n}$. We see that $\left(q_{n}\right)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a decreasing sequence which converges to $\0$ pointwise on the dense set $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, hence $q_{n}\downarrow \0$. Note that $q_{n}\left(0\right)=2$ and $q_{n}\left(\frac{1}{m}\right) > 0$, for all $m,n\in \mathbb{N}$.

Fix $n\in \mathbb{N}$. The set $U := q_{n}^{-1}\left(1,+\8\right)$ is an open neighborhood of $0$, hence there is $k\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\ge k}\subseteq U$.
For every $l\in \{1,\ldots,k-1\}$ we have $q_{n}\left(\frac{1}{l}\right) > 0$, and since $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is pointwise null on $\left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$, there is $\alpha_{l}$ such that $e_{\alpha}\left(\frac{1}{l}\right)\le q_{n}\left(\frac{1}{l}\right)$, whenever $\alpha\ge\alpha_{l}$. Find $\alpha_{0}\ge\alpha_{1},\ldots ,\alpha_{k-1}$. Then, if $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$ and $l \in \{1,\ldots, k-1\}$, we have $e_{\alpha}\left(\frac{1}{l}\right)\le q_{n}\left(\frac{1}{l}\right)$; if $x\in \left\{\frac{1}{m}\right\}_{m\ge k}\cup\left\{0\right\}$, then $e_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\le 1<q_{n}\left(x\right)$. In summary, $e_{\alpha}\le q_{n}$ when $\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}$, and so $\left\{q_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ witnesses directed order convergence of $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ to $\0$.
\qed
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{csp}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ has the countable supremum property (CSP), i.e.\ if $Q\subseteq E$ is such that $\bigwedge Q=0_{E}$, there is a countable $Q'\subseteq Q$ such that $\bigwedge Q'=0_{E}$;
\item[(ii)] $E$ has the directed countable supremum property, i.e.\ if $Q\subseteq E$ is such that $Q\downarrow 0_{E}$, there is a countable $Q'\subseteq Q$ such that $\bigwedge Q'=0_{E}$ (in this case $Q'$ may be taken to be a decreasing sequence);
\item[(iii)] $E^{\delta}$ has the CSP;
\item[(iv)] Each order bounded disjoint set in $E$ is countable;
\item[(v)] Order convergence and $\sigma$-order convergence agree on $E$;
\item[(vi)] Order convergence and directed $\sigma$-order convergence agree on $E$.
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) follows from the fact that, for $Q\subseteq E$, we have $\bigwedge_{E} Q=0_{E}$ if and only if $\bigwedge_{E^{\delta}} Q=0_{E^{\delta}}$.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Existence of some countable $Q'\subseteq Q$ with $\bigwedge Q'=0_{E}$ follows immediately from (i). If $Q'=\left\{q_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, we can construct a sequence $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq Q$ as follows. Let $e_{1}:=q_{1}$, and if $e_{1},\dots,e_{n}$ are already selected, then since $Q$ is directed downward, it contains some $e_{n+1}\le e_{n},q_{n+1}$. It is easy to see that $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}e_{n}=0_{E}$.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): It follows from Theorem~\ref{pervasive} that $E$ is an order dense subspace of $E^{\delta}$. Suppose that $P\subseteq E^{\delta}$ is such that $\bigwedge P=0_{E^{\delta}}$. According to Corollary~\ref{pervdird} applied to $P^{\wedge}$, there is $Q\subseteq E\cap \bigcup_{p\in P^{\wedge}}\left(p+E_{+}^{\delta}\right)$ such that $Q\downarrow 0_{E^{\delta}}$. By our assumption, there is a countable $Q'\subseteq Q$ such that $Q'\downarrow 0_{E}$. For every $q\in Q'$ there is a finite $P_{q}\subseteq P$ such that $\bigwedge P_{q}\le q$. It follows now that $P':=\bigcup_{q\in Q'}P_{q}$ is countable, and it is easy to see that $\bigwedge P'=0_{E^{\delta}}$.

(iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv): According to \cite[Theorem~29.3]{lz}, $E^{\delta}$ has the CSP if and only if each disjoint order bounded set there is countable. Clearly, this condition implies (iv). For the converse, note that if $D\subseteq E^{\delta}_{+}\setminus\left\{0_{E^{\delta}}\right\}$ is disjoint, uncountable and order bounded, then for every $d\in D$ there is $e_{d}\in E\cap \left(0_{E^{\delta}},d\right]$; then $\left\{e_{d}:d\in D\right\}$ is disjoint, uncountable and order bounded in $E$, which is a contradiction.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(vi) follows from the definitions and the fact that order and directed order convergences agree on pervasive spaces (Proposition~\ref{o=do}). (vi)$\Rightarrow$(v) follows from the fact that $\sigma$-order convergence is stronger than order convergence, but weaker than directed $\sigma$-order convergence.

(v)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Assume that $Q\subseteq E$ is such that $Q\downarrow 0_{E}$. Then, $Q\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, hence $Q\xrightarrow[]{\sigma\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$, and so there is a countable $P\subseteq E$ such that $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$, and $P$ dominates the tails of $Q$. This means that for every $p\in P$ there is $q_{p}\in Q$ with $q_{p}\le p$. It now follows that $Q':=\left\{q_{p}:p\in P\right\}$ is a countable subset of $Q$ with $\bigwedge Q'=0_{E}$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{sosdo}
Recall that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a filter on a set $X$, then $r\in \mathbb{R}$ is the limit of $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ along $\mathcal{F}$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have $f^{-1}\left(r-\varepsilon,r+\varepsilon\right)\in\mathcal{F}$. It is easy to see that the limit defined this way is unique, and if $\mathcal{F}$ is an ultrafilter and $f$ is bounded, then the limit along $\mathcal{F}$ always exists (see \cite[17.5(ii)]{schechter}).

Let $F$ be the space of all bounded Borel functions on $\left(0,1\right]$. Since $\left(\left(0,r\right]\right)_{0<r\le 1}$ is a decreasing net of subsets of $\left(0,1\right]$, there is an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\left(0,1\right]$ which contains each subset. Taking a limit with respect to $\mathcal{U}$ defines a vector lattice homomorphism from $\ell_{\8}\left(0,1\right]$ into $\mathbb{R}$. We denote its restriction to $F$ by $\varphi$. For every $t\in \left(0,1\right]$ we have that $\varphi\left(\1_{\left(0,t\right]}\right)=\varphi\left(\1_{\left(0,t\right)}\right)=1$, hence $\1_{\left\{t\right\}}\in\ker\varphi$.

Let us show that $E:=\left\{f\in F: \varphi\left(f\right)=\int f\right\}$ is order dense in $F$. Indeed, if $f>\0$, there is $t\in \left(0,1\right]$ such that $r:=f\left(t\right)>0$. Then, $f\ge r\1_{\left\{t\right\}}$, and since $\1_{\left\{t\right\}}\in\ker\varphi$ and $\int \1_{\left\{t\right\}}=0$, we conclude that $r\1_{\left\{t\right\}}\in E$.
