Also, clearly $\1\in E$ is an order unit.

We order $\mathcal{U}$ by reverse inclusion, and for $U\in\mathcal{U}$ let $x_{U}$ be an arbitrary point in $U$. Let us show that for every $f\in F$ we have $\lim_{U\in \mathcal{U}}f\left(x_{U}\right)=\lim_{\mathcal{U}}f=\varphi\left(f\right)$. Indeed, for every $\varepsilon>0$, by the definition of the limit with respect to a filter, we get
\[U_{\varepsilon}:=f^{-1}\left(\varphi\left(f\right)-\varepsilon,\varphi\left(f\right)+\varepsilon\right)\in\mathcal{U};\]
then, for every $U\subseteq U_{\varepsilon}$ we have $x_{U}\in U\subseteq U_{\varepsilon}$, and so $\left|f\left(x_{U}\right)-\varphi\left(f\right)\right|<\varepsilon$. Therefore, for every $f\in E$ we have $\int f=\varphi\left(f\right)=\lim_{U\in \mathcal{U}}f\left(x_{U}\right)$.

Let us show that $\left(\1_{\left\{x_{U}\right\}}\right)_{U\in\mathcal{U}}$ is not $\mathrm{d\sigma o}$-null. Assume that $\left\{h_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq E$ is decreasing with $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}h_{n}=\0$ and dominates the tails of our net. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we have that $\1_{\left\{x_{U}\right\}}\le h_{n}$, hence $h_{n}\left(x_{U}\right)\ge 1$ for small enough $U$. It follows that $\int h_{n}=\lim_{U\in \mathcal{U}}h_{n}\left(x_{U}\right)\ge 1$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. On the other hand, as $E$ is order dense in $F$, it follows from Corollary~\ref{odm} that $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}h_{n}=\0$ in $F$. Since the infimum of a countable collection of Borel functions is its pointwise infimum, we conclude that $h_{n}\left(x\right)\downarrow 0$, for every $x\in\left(0,1\right]$. As a result, we get $1\le \int h_{n}\downarrow 0$, contradiction.

Finally, we prove that $\1_{\left\{x_{U}\right\}}\xrightarrow[]{\sigma\mathrm{o}}\0$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ let $A_{n}:=\left(0,\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right]$, $B_{n}:=\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right]$ and $g_{n}:=\1_{A_{n}}+\left(2^{n}-1\right)\1_{B_{n}}$. We have that $\varphi\left(g_{n}\right)=1=\int g_{n}$, hence $g_{n}\in E$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Moreover, $\bigwedge_{n\in\mathbb{N}}g_{n}=\0$ pointwise, hence in $E$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ take $A_{n}\in\mathcal{U}$ as an index. Then, for every $U\subseteq A_{n}$ we have $x_{U}\in U\subseteq A_{n}$, hence $\1_{\left\{x_{U}\right\}}\le \1_{A_{n}}\le g_{n}$. Thus, $\left\{g_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ dominates the tails of our net.
\qed
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{socomp}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is $\sigma$-order locally pre-compact;
\item[(ii)] Every order interval in $E$ is $\sigma$-order pre-compact;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is atomic and has the CSP;
\item[(iv)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{X}_{csp}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$.
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) is proved analogously to the corresponding equivalence in Theorem~\ref{ordprec}.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): Let us first show that $E$ satisfies the condition (ii) of Proposition~\ref{csp}. Assume that $Q\downarrow 0_{E}$. Without loss of generality we may assume that this net is contained in an order interval, and so contains a $\sigma$-order Cauchy subnet $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$. There is a countable $P\subseteq E$ with $\bigwedge P=0_{E}$ which dominates the tails of $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$. For every $p\in P$ there is $\alpha_{p}$ such that $e_{\alpha_{p}}-e_{\alpha}\le p$, for every $\alpha\ge\alpha_{p}$; in fact, since $e_{\alpha}\downarrow 0_{E}$, it follows that $e_{\alpha_{p}}\le p$. Then, $Q':=\left\{e_{\alpha_{p}}:p\in P\right\}$ is a countable subset of $Q$ with $\bigwedge Q'=0_{E}$.

It now follows from Proposition~\ref{csp} that order and $\sigma$-order convergences agree on $E$. In particular, every order interval in $E$ is order pre-compact, and so $E$ is atomic, according to Theorem~\ref{ordprec}. The converse is proved by reversing the last two arguments.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv): According to Theorem~\ref{ordprec}, $E$ is isomorphic to a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$, for some set $X$, with $\1_{\left\{x\right\}}\in E$ for every $x\in X$. Since $E$ also has the CSP, in light of condition (iv) in Proposition~\ref{csp}, $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{X}_{csp}$. The converse is straightforward.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{socomp2}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is $\sigma$-order locally compact;
\item[(ii)] Every order interval in $E$ is $\sigma$-order compact;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice with the CSP;
\item[(iv)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as an ideal of $\mathbb{R}^{X}_{csp}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) is proved analogously to the corresponding equivalence in Theorem~\ref{ordprec}. (iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv) follows from combining Proposition~\ref{socomp} with \cite[Theorem~1.40]{ab0}, while the converse is straightforward.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): It follows from Proposition~\ref{socomp} that $E$ has the CSP, and so order and $\sigma$-order convergences agree on $E$. Hence, order intervals in $E$ are order compact, and so, by Corollary~\ref{automaticlat}, $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice. The converse is proved by reversing these arguments.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The analogues of the conditions (i) and (ii) in Proposition~\ref{socomp} and Corollary~\ref{socomp2} but for directed $\sigma$-order convergence can be added to the lists.
\qed
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{rucomp}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is relatively uniformly locally pre-compact;
\item[(ii)] Every order interval in $E$ is relatively uniformly pre-compact;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is atomic and such that order and relative uniform convergences agree on $E$;
\item[(iv)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$ and such that every $e\in E$ is majorated by an element of $E$.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii) is proved analogously to the corresponding equivalence in Theorem~\ref{ordprec}.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): Arguing as in the proof of the corresponding implication in Proposition~\ref{socomp}, one can show that any $Q\downarrow 0_{E}$ contains an $\mathrm{ru}$-null sequence. This fact can then be leveraged to show that $\mathrm{ru}=\mathrm{do}$ on $E$. By Proposition~\ref{o=do}, we conclude that $\mathrm{ru}=\mathrm{o}$ on $E$, and in particular, order intervals in $E$ are order pre-compact. Thus, $E$ is atomic, by virtue of Theorem~\ref{ordprec}. By reversing the latter two arguments we get (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii).

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv): First, since $E$ is atomic, by Theorem~\ref{ordprec} we may assume that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ for some set $X$, with $\1_{\left\{x\right\}}\in E$ for every $x\in X$. Moreover, order convergence agrees with pointwise convergence in order bounded subsets of $E$. The last condition is trivially satisfied if $X$ is finite, and so we assume otherwise.

Let $e\in E_{+}$. Let $A$ be the collection of all finite subsets of $X$. For $\alpha\in A$ define $e_{\alpha}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ by $e_{\alpha}\left(x\right):=\frac{e\left(x\right)}{\left|\alpha\right|}$ if $x\in\alpha$, and $e_{\alpha}\left(x\right):=e\left(x\right)$, otherwise. Then, $\operatorname{supp} \left(e-e_{\alpha}\right)$ is finite, hence $e-e_{\alpha}\in E$, and so $e_{\alpha}\in E$.

Clearly, $e_{\alpha}\to\0$ pointwise, therefore in order, hence relatively uniformly. Thus, there is $g\in E_{+}$ such that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $\alpha$ such that $e_{\alpha}\le \frac{1}{n}g$, and so, for all $x\notin\alpha$, we have $e\left(x\right)=e_{\alpha}\left(x\right)\le \frac{1}{n}g\left(x\right)$. Since $\alpha$ is a finite set, it follows that $g$ majorates $e$.

If $f\in E$, find $e\in E_{+}$ such that $\pm f\le e$, and $g\in E_{+}$ which majorates $e$. It is clear that $g$ also majorates $f$.

(iv)$\Rightarrow$(iii): Suppose that $e_{\alpha}\downarrow \0$. Without loss of generality we may assume that this net is bounded above by some $e\in E_{+}$. Let $g$ be a majorant of $e$. Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$. There are $x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\in X$ such that $\frac{1}{n}g\left(x\right)\ge e\left(x\right)$, for all $x\notin\left\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\right\}$. Since $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)$ converges to $\0$ pointwise, there is $\alpha_{n}$ such that $e_{\alpha}\left(x_{k}\right)\le \frac{1}{n}g\left(x_{k}\right)$, whenever $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$ and $k\in\left\{1,\dots,m\right\}$. It now follows that $e_{\alpha}\le \frac{1}{n}g$ as soon as $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$. Since $n$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{ru}}\0$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{rucomp2}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $E$ is relatively uniformly locally compact;
\item[(ii)] Every order interval in $E$ is relatively uniformly compact;
\item[(iii)] $E$ is an atomic Dedekind complete vector lattice such that order and relative uniform convergences agree on $E$;
\item[(iv)] There is a set $X$ such that $E$ embeds as an ideal of $\mathbb{R}^{X}$ with $c_{00}\left(X\right)\subseteq E$ and such that every $e\in E$ is majorated by an element of $E$.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
Both $\mathbb{R}^{X}_{csp}$ and $c_{0}\left(X\right)$ satisfy the conditions of Corollary~\ref{rucomp2} for arbitrary $X$. Indeed, any $f\in c_{0}\left(X\right)$ is majorated by $\sqrt{\left|f\right|}$; any $f\in \mathbb{R}^{X}_{csp}$ is majorated by $\left|f\right|g$, where $\operatorname{supp} f=\left\{x_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$, and $g\in\mathbb{R}^{X}$ is such that $g\left(x_{n}\right)=n$. Another example is the space of all real sequences of polynomial growth. The atomic order continuous Banach lattices form another class of examples, since on such spaces order and relative uniform convergences agree (see \cite[Proposition~3]{bw}). An example of a space which satisfies the conditions of Corollary~\ref{socomp2} but not of Proposition~\ref{rucomp} is $\ell_{\8}$.
\qed
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{T:rep of o.u.s.}\interlinepenalty=10000
Let $\left(E,e\right)$ be an order unit space. Then:
\item[(i)] $f\mapsto \hat{f}$ is an isometric order isomorphism from $E$ onto a norm-dense subspace of $\operatorname{Aff}\left(K_{E},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.
\item[(ii)] $f\mapsto \hat{f}|_{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E}}$ is an isometric order isomorphism from $E$ onto a supremum-dense subspace of $\mathcal{C}\left(\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{apm}
We have $a^{+}\wedge_{A_{+}}a^{-}=0_{A}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
First, it is clear that $U_{a^{+}}a^{-}=0_{A}=U_{a^{-}}a^{+}$. Assume that $0_{A}\le b\le a^{+},a^{-}$. Then, $0_{A}\le U_{a^{+}}b\le U_{a^{+}}a^{-}=0_{A}$. Hence, $U_{a^{+}}b=0_{A}$, implying $U_{b}a^{+}=0_{A}$ (see \cite[Lemma~1.26]{as}). Therefore, $0_{A}\le b^{3}=U_{b}b\le U_{b}a^{+}=0_{A}$, thus $b^{3}=0_{A}$, and so $b=0_{A}$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
\label{normal}
A functional on a JBW-algebra is normal if and only if it is directed order continuous.
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Sufficiency was already addressed above. For necessity, note that by \cite[Proposition~2.52]{as} any normal functional is a difference of positive normal functionals. The latter two are directed order continuous by Proposition~\ref{docont}, and so is their difference.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{jblat}
For a JB-algebra $A$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $A$ is Jordan isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}_{0}\left(X\right)$ for some locally compact Hausdorff space $X$;
\item[(ii)] $A$ is associative;
\item[(iii)] $A$ is a vector lattice;
\item[(iv)] $A$ satisfies the Riesz decomposition property, i.e.\ $\left[0_{A},a\right]+\left[0_{A},b\right]=\left[0_{A},a+b\right]$, for every $a,b\in A_{+}$;
\item[(v)] $A^{**}$ is a vector lattice;
\item[(vi)] $A$ is pervasive;
\item[(vii)] $A$ is weakly pervasive.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii), as well as (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv) and (iii)$\Rightarrow$(vi) are trivial. (vi)$\Rightarrow$(vii) follows from Theorem~\ref{pervasive} or results in \cite{km}. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is \cite[Theorem~3.2.2]{hs}. (vii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) follows from combining Lemmas~\ref{wp} and~\ref{apm}.

                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                

(iv)$\Rightarrow$(v): First, note that the order on $A^{**}$ as a JB-algebra is determined by normal states, and in particular, is consistent with its order as a dual of an ordered vector space $A^{*}$. Since for every $a\in A$ we have that $A_{+}\ni \sqrt{a^{2}}\ge a$ (here we use \cite[Theorem~3.2.2]{hs} for $\mathrm{JB}\left(a\right)$), it follows that $A$ is a directed ordered vector space. Moreover, since $A$ satisfies the Riesz decomposition property, $A_{+}$ is norm-closed in $A$, and the norm is monotone on $A_{+}$, by \cite[Theorem~2.47 and Exercise~2.17]{at}, it follows that $A^{*}$ is a vector lattice endowed with a norm equivalent to a Banach lattice norm. We conclude that $A^{**}$ is also a lattice (see \cite[Theorem~4.1]{ab}).

(v)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Since $A$ is a subalgebra of $A^{**}$, it is enough to show that $A^{**}$ is associative. Moreover, recall that the latter is always unital. Let $K_{A^{**}}$ be the space of states on $A^{**}$, and let $K$ be the collection of the pure states, i.e.\ the extreme points of $K_{A^{**}}$. According to \cite[Theorem~2.5.6]{kv}, $K$ is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-closed in $K_{A^{**}}$ and the representation $a\mapsto \hat{a}$ as in Theorem~\ref{T:rep of o.u.s.} is an isometric vector lattice homomorphism onto $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$. Moreover, $1_{A^{**}}$ is mapped into $\1$. Since any unital isometry between JB-algebras is a Jordan isomorphism (see \cite[Theorem~4]{wy}), $A^{**}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$, and in particular it is associative.\begin{comment}
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
            
                                                                                                                                                                                 

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         

              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
            
                                                                                                                  

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
\end{comment}
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{unital}
Let $\left(E,e\right)$ and $\left(F,f\right)$ be order unit spaces, and let $T\colon E\to F$ be a linear operator. Then:
\item[(i)] If $T$ is unital, then it is positive if and only if $\|T\|=1$.
\item[(ii)] If $T$ is a bijection, then any two of being unital, being an order isomorphism and being an isometry imply the third one.
\item[(iii)] If $T$ is unital, then it is an isometry if and only if it is an order embedding.
\item[(iv)] If $F=\mathbb{R}$, then any two of being unital, positivity and having norm $1$ imply the third one.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
(i): Necessity follows from $T\mathrm{B}_{E}=T\left[-e,e\right]\subseteq\left[-f,f\right]=\mathrm{B}_{F}$. For sufficiency, let $g\in E_{+}$. We may assume that $\|g\|\le 2$, so that $g\in \left[0_{E},2e\right]=e+\left[-e,e\right]$. Then, $Tg\in Te+T\left[-e,e\right]\subseteq f+\left[-f,f\right]\subseteq F_{+}$.

(ii): The facts that every unital order isomorphism is an isometry, and every unital isometry is an order isomorphism follow from applying (i) to $T$ and $T^{-1}$. If $T$ is an isometric order isomorphism, we have that $T\left[-e,e\right]= \left[-f,f\right]$, and since $e=\max \left[-e,e\right]$, it follows that $Te=\max \left[-f,f\right]=f$.

(iii) follows from (ii) applied to $E$ and $\left(TE,f\right)$.

(iv): In view of (i), it is enough to show that a positive functional of norm $1$ is unital, which is done using a similar argument as in (ii).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
\label{face}
Let $E$ be an ordered vector space. For a cone $C\subseteq E_{+}$ the following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $C$ is a face of $E_{+}$;
\item[(ii)] If $e,f\in E_{+}$ are such that $e+f\in C$, then $e,f\in C$;
\item[(iii)] $C$ is a lower set in $E_{+}$, i.e.\ $0_{E}\le e\le f\in C$ implies $e\in C$;
\item[(iv)] $C$ is a full set;
\item[(v)] There is a directed full subspace $H\subseteq E$ such that $C=H_{+}$.
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): Since $C$ is a cone, we have that $\frac{1}{2}e+\frac{1}{2}f\in C$, hence $e,f\in C$.

(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii): We have that $e,f-e\in E_{+}$, and $e+\left(f-e\right)=f\in C$ implying $e\in C$.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i): Assume that $e,f\in E_{+}$ and $t\in\left(0,1\right)$ are such that $te+\left(1-t\right)f\in C$. Then, $0_{E}\le e\le \frac{1}{t}\left( te+\left(1-t\right)f\right)\in C$ implies $e\in C$. Similarly, $f\in C$, and so $C$ is a face of $E_{+}$.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(v): It is clear that $H:=C-C$ is a directed subspace of $E$. Let us show that $H_{+}=C$. If $f,e\in C$ with $f-e\ge 0_{E}$, then $0_{E}\le f-e\le f\in C$ implies $f-e\in C$, so that $H_{+}\subseteq C$. The converse inclusion is obvious.

If $e,f\in H$ with $e\le f$, then $f-e\in H_{+}=C$, therefore $\left[0_{E},f-e\right]\subseteq C$, and so $\left[e,f\right]=e+\left[0_{E},f-e\right]\subseteq C-C$. We conclude that $H=C-C$ is a full subspace.

                                                                                                          

(v)$\Rightarrow$(iv)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is straightforward.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
The collection of nonempty faces $C$ of $E_{+}$ is order isomorphic to the collection of directed full linear subspaces $H$ of $E$ via $C\mapsto C-C$ and $H\mapsto H_{+}$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{atmo}
Let $E$ be an ordered vector space and let $e>0_{E}$. Then:
\item[(i)] $e$ is an atom if and only if $\left[0,+\8\right)e$ is an extreme ray.
\item[(ii)] $E$ is atomic if and only if every nonempty and nonzero face of $E_{+}$ contains an extreme ray.
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
(i): Necessity: If $e$ is an atom, then $\left[0,1\right]e$ is a lower set in $E_{+}$, hence so is $\left[0,+\8\right)e$, and so the latter is a face of $E_{+}$ by Proposition~\ref{face}.

Sufficiency: If $\left[0,+\8\right)e$ is an extreme ray, it is a face of $E_{+}$. Hence, $\left[0_{E},e\right]\subseteq \left[0,+\8\right)e$, and so $\left[0_{E},e\right]\subseteq \left[0,1\right]e$.

(ii): Necessity: If $C\subseteq E_{+}$ is a face which contains $f>0_{E}$, then there is an atom $e\in\left(0_{E},f\right]\subseteq C$. It follows from (i) that $\left[0,+\8\right)e$ is an extreme ray of $E_{+}$ contained in $C$.

Sufficiency: If $f>0_{E}$, then $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[0_{E},nf\right]$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition~\ref{face}, and so is a face. By our assumption and (i), this face contains an atom, say $e$. Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be such that $e\in\left[0_{E},nf\right]$. Then, $\frac{1}{n}e$ is an atom contained in $\left[0_{E},f\right]$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
\label{minext}
Assume that $E$ is Archimedean. Then, $C\subseteq E_{+}$ is an extreme ray if and only if it is a minimal nonzero face.
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Since an extreme ray is one-dimensional, and any face of a cone is a cone, necessity is clear. For sufficiency, assume that $C$ is a minimal nonzero face of $E_{+}$.

Suppose that $C$ is not a ray, so that there are two linearly independent vectors $u,v\in C$. Let $F:=\operatorname{span}\left\{u,v\right\}$, which is an Archimedean ordered vector space. Then, $F_{+}:=E_{+}\cap F$ is closed with respect to the unique Hausdorff linear topology on the two-dimensional space $F$, and it is not a ray since it contains $u,v$. We clearly have $C\cap F\subseteq E_{+}\cap F=F_{+}$. For the converse inclusion, assume that $t,s\in\mathbb{R}$ are such that $tu+sv=:e\in E_{+}$. Then, either $t,s\ge 0$, and then clearly $e\in C$, or say $t>0>s$, so that $C\ni u=\frac{1}{t}e+\frac{-s}{t}v$ implies $e\in C$.

Since $F_{+}$ is a proper cone but not a ray, there exists $0_E < f \in \partial{F_{+}}\subseteq C$. It follows from minimality that $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left[0_{E},nf\right]=C\supseteq F_{+}$. Hence, $f$ is an order unit of $F$ implying that $f$ belongs to the relative interior of $F_+$ in $F$ (see \cite[Proposition~1.5.11(i)]{kv}). This contradicts $f \in \partial F_+$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The assumption that $E$ is Archimedean in Proposition~\ref{minext} is not superfluous: consider $E=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ ordered by the cone $C:=\mathbb{R}\times\left(0,+\8\right)\cup\left\{\left(0,0\right)\right\}$, which has only two nonempty faces: $C$ and $\left\{\left(0,0\right)\right\}$.
\qed
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
A slightly different (but essentially equivalent) notion of an ice cream cone exists in the literature, see \cite[Section~2.6]{at}. If $F$ is a Hilbert space, then $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is called a \emph{spin factor}. A term sometimes used for $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ in the general case is \emph{generalized spin factor}.
\qed
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Note that $F\times \left[0,+\8\right)\subseteq  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ can be identified with the collection of all closed balls in $F$, endowed with the structure of a metric ordered cone: the addition and positive multiplication are defined in terms of the algebraic operations with sets in a vector space, the ordering is by inclusion and the distance is the Hausdorff metric. It was observed in \cite{schmidt} that the correspondence $\left(f,r\right)\mapsto\mathrm{B}\left(f,r\right)$ is an order isomorphism, an isometry, and an algebraic isomorphism.
\qed
<!-- end remark-7 -->

<!-- proposition-33: body_md -->
Isometric order isomorphisms between ice cream spaces are precisely the maps induced by isometric isomorphisms between the underlying normed spaces.
<!-- end proposition-33 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a Banach space. It is clear that any isometric isomorphism from $F$ onto $G$ induces an isometric order isomorphism from $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ onto $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(G\right)$. For the converse, suppose that $T\colon 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)\to  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(G\right)$ is an isometric order isomorphism. Then, by part~(ii) of Lemma~\ref{unital}, $T$ is unital, i.e.\ $T\left(0_{F},1\right)=\left(0_{G},1\right)$.

Fix $f\in F$. We have that $\left(f,\|f\|\right)\in\partial  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$, hence $T\left(f,\|f\|\right)\in\partial  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(G\right)_{+}$. Therefore, $T\left(f,\|f\|\right)=\left(g,\|g\|\right)$, for some $g\in G$ with $\|g\|=\|f\|$. Then,
\[T\left(f,0\right)=T\left(f,\|f\|\right)-T\left(0_{F},\|f\|\right)=\left(g,\|g\|\right)-\left(0_{G},\|f\|\right)=\left(g,0\right).\]
Since $f\in F$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $T$ isometrically maps $F$ into $G$. Applying the same argument to $T^{-1}$ shows that $S:=\left.T\right|_{F}$ is an isometric isomorphism onto $G$, and $T=S\oplus \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbb{R}}$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-34: body_md -->
\label{icecream} Let $F$ be a normed space.
\item[(i)] $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)^{*}=F^{*}\oplus_{\8}\mathbb{R}$ order isometrically with respect to the ice cream order on the latter.
\item[(ii)] The states on $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ are the functionals of the form $\left(\nu,1\right)$, where $\nu\in \mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. The pure states are the functionals of the form $\left(\nu,1\right)$, where $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$.
\item[(iii)] $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is order isometric to a supremum-dense subspace of $\mathcal{C}\left(\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.
\item[(iv)] If $F$ is norm complete, $\dim F>0$ and $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, then $F$ is non-reflexive if and only if there exists a strictly positive pure state on $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$.
<!-- end proposition-34 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
(i): The only non-straightforward part of the statement is showing that the two spaces are order isomorphic. We have that $\left<\left(f^{*},s\right),\left(f,r\right)\right>=\left<f^{*},f\right>+sr$. If $\|f^{*}\|\le s$ and $\|f\|\le r$, then $sr\ge -\left<f^{*},f\right>$, and so $\left<\left(f^{*},s\right),\left(f,r\right)\right>\ge 0$. If $\|f^{*}\|> s$, there is $f\in F$ such that $\|f\|=1$ and $\left<f^{*},f\right><-s$, and then $\left(f,1\right)\ge 0$ but $\left<\left(f^{*},s\right),\left(f,1\right)\right>=\left<f^{*},f\right>+s<0$.

(ii): Let $\left(\nu,r\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)^{*}$. This functional is a state if and only if $\left(\nu,r\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)^{*}_{+}$ and $\left(\nu,r\right)\left(0_{F},1\right)=1$, i.e.\ $r=1$; by (i), this is equivalent to $\|\nu\|\le r=1$. The second claim follows from the first one.

(iii) follows from (ii) and part~(ii) of Theorem~\ref{T:rep of o.u.s.}.

(iv): First, since $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, we have $\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}=\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$, and so the pure states on $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ are precisely the functionals $\left(\nu,1\right)$, where $\nu\in \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$.

Let us show that $\left(\nu,1\right)$, where $\nu\in \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$, is strictly positive if and only if $\nu$ does not attain its norm. Strict positivity means that $\left(\nu,1\right)\left(f,r\right)=\nu\left(f\right)+r>0$, whenever $f\in F$ and $r>0$ are such that $\|f\|\le r$. Attainment of the norm for $\nu$ means existence of $f\in\mathrm{S}_{F}$ such that $\nu\left(f\right)=-1$, equivalently $\left(\nu,1\right)\left(f,1\right)=0$.

It follows that a strictly positive pure state on $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ exists if and only if some $\nu\in \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ does not attain its norm. By James' Theorem (see \cite[Corollary~3.131]{fhhmz}), this last condition is equivalent to $F$ not being reflexive.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\label{lur}
If $F$ is a Banach space with a separable dual, by \cite[Theorem~8.7]{fhhmz}, it has an equivalent norm such that $F^{*}$ is \emph{locally uniformly rotund (LUR)}, i.e.\ whenever $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq F$ and $f\in F$ are such that $2\|f_{n}\|^{2}+2\|f\|^{2}-\|f_{n}+f\|^{2}\to 0$, it follows that $f_{n}\to f$. Note that if $F^{*}$ is LUR, then it is strictly convex (this can be deduced from \cite[Fact~7.7]{fhhmz}).
\qed
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
In part~(iv) of Proposition~\ref{icecream} it was established that pure states on ice cream spaces can be strictly positive. Note that this situation cannot occur even for limits of pure states on pervasive order unit spaces. Indeed, assume that $\left(E,e\right)$ is such a space, with $\dim E>1$, and $\nu\in \overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E}$. By part~(ii) of Theorem~\ref{T:rep of o.u.s.}, we have that $E$ embeds as a supremum-dense subspace of $\mathcal{C}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E}\bigr)$. According to Proposition~\ref{arch1}, $E$ is in fact order dense in $\mathcal{C}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E}\bigr)$. Take $\0<f\in \mathcal{C}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{ext}}^{\mathrm{w}^{*}}K_{E}\bigr)$ which vanishes at $\nu$. Then, there is $0_{E}<e\in E$ such that $e\le f$, and so $\nu\left(e\right)=0$. Thus, $\nu$ is not strictly positive.
\qed
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-35: body_md -->
\label{iceaff}
Let $F$ be a normed space.
\item[(i)] $ 
  \mathord{

      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    }

\left(F\right)$ is order isometric to a norm-dense subspace of $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$ endowed with the pointwise order and supremum norm.
\item[(ii)] $

(ii): By (i) we have that $

    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);

  } 
\left(F^{*}\right)\simeq \operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{**}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$. Since by Goldstine's theorem (see \cite[Theorem~3.96]{fhhmz}) we have that $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ is dense in $\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{**}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$, we can identify $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{**}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$ with the set of all $e\in \operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\mathrm{w}\right)$ that can be continuously extended to $\mathrm{B}_{F^{**}}$. It is also clear that $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\mathrm{w}\right)\subseteq \operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\|\cdot\|\right)$, which in turn is contained in the space of all bounded affine functions on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. Assume that $u$ is a bounded affine function on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and let $v:=u-u\left(0_{F}\right)\1$, which is also a bounded affine function on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. This function satisfies $v\left(0_{F}\right)=0$, and for every $f\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $t\in\left[0,1\right]$ we have that
\[v\left(tf\right)=tv\left(f\right)+\left(1-t\right)v\left(0_{F}\right)=tv\left(f\right).\] Moreover, for $f,g\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ we have $v\left(\frac{1}{2}f+\frac{1}{2}g\right)=\frac{1}{2}v\left(f\right)+\frac{1}{2}v\left(g\right)$. It is easy to see that extending $v$ by positive homogeneity yields a linear functional on $F$. This functional is bounded on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$, so is an element of $F^{*}$. Hence, we may view $v$ as a $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-continuous linear functional on $F^{**}$, and so $u=v+u\left(0_{F}\right)\1\in\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{**}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.

<!-- proposition-38: body_md -->
\label{bw}
\item[(i)] Viewing $F^{*}\subseteq \mathcal{C}\left(F\right)$ or $F^{*}\subseteq \mathcal{C}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F}\right)$, the restriction of the compact-open topology agrees with the $\mathrm{bw}^{*}$-topology.
\item[(ii)] $\left(F^{*},\mathrm{bw}^{*}\right)^{*}=F$.
<!-- end proposition-38 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
For (ii), as well as the case of $\mathcal{C}\left(F\right)$ in (i), see \cite[Lemmas~8.45 and~8.46]{at}. Also, it is easy to see that the restriction map $R\colon\mathcal{C}\left(F\right)\to\mathcal{C}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F}\right)$ defined by $\varphi\mapsto \varphi|_{\mathrm{B}_{F}}$ is a continuous map with respect to compact-open topologies. Clearly, $R|_{F^{*}}$ is injective. To show that $R|_{F^{*}}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, let $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ be a net in $F^{*}$ such that $\bigl(f^{*}_{\alpha}|_{\mathrm{B}_{F}}\bigr)_{\alpha\in A}$ is $\mathrm{bw}^{*}$-null and let $K\subseteq F$ be compact. There is $r>0$ such that $rK\subseteq \mathrm{B}_{F}$, and so $f^{*}_{\alpha}|_{\mathrm{B}_{F}}\to\0$ uniformly on $rK$. Due to linearity, we have that $f^{*}_{\alpha}\to\0$ uniformly on $K$, and since $K$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $f^{*}_{\alpha}\to\0$.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- proposition-39: body_md -->
\label{iceo}
\item[(i)] The weak and pointwise topologies coincide on $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$. The $\mathrm{w}^{*}$- and pointwise topologies coincide on $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\|\cdot\|\right)$.
\item[(ii)] Bounded pointwise convergence, bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-convergence, bounded compact-open convergence and continuous convergence agree on $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\|\cdot\|\right)$.
\item[(iii)] The bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology agrees with the compact-open topology on $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\|\cdot\|\right)$.
<!-- end proposition-39 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
The first claim in (i) follows from part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{icecream}, and so in this proof we will be only working with $E:=\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F},\|\cdot\|\right)$.

(i): Recall that $\left(\nu,r\right)\left(f,s\right)=\nu\left(f\right)+rs$, where $\left(\nu,r\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F^{*}\right)$ and $\left(f,s\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$. Hence, if we identify $\left(\nu,r\right)$ with $\nu+r\1$, then $\left(f,1\right)$ acts on it as the evaluation at $f$, for $f\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$. This shows that the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology is stronger than the pointwise topology on $E$. On the other hand, since $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)=\operatorname{span}\left\{\left(f,1\right): f\in\mathrm{B}_{F}\right\}$, we get the converse relation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      

(ii): It follows from (i) that bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$- and bounded pointwise convergences coincide on $E$. Continuous convergence is always stronger than compact-open convergence (see \cite[Proposition~8.2]{btw}), which in turn is stronger than pointwise convergence.

Let $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ be a net, and for every $\alpha\in A$ write $e_{\alpha}=f^{*}_{\alpha}+e_{\alpha}\left(0_{F}\right)\1$, where $f^{*}_{\alpha}\in F^{*}$. Assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ converges to $\0$ with respect to continuous convergence. Then, $e_{\alpha}\left(0_{F}\right)\to 0$, and so $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ also converges to $\0$ with respect to continuous convergence. It follows from the discussion at the start of Subsection~\ref{iceoc} that $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is eventually norm-bounded. We conclude that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is eventually norm-bounded, hence bounded compact-open-null. Similarly, if $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is bounded pointwise-null, then $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-null, hence null with respect to continuous convergence, which also implies that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ converges to $\0$ with respect to continuous convergence.

(iii): Recall that the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology on $E$ is with respect to $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$, and so, by renorming the latter, we may represent $E\simeq \left(F\oplus_{\8} \mathbb{R}\right)^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{C}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]\right)$. Recall that by part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{bw}, the bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology on $E$ coincides with the compact-open topology viewing $E\subseteq\mathcal{C}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]\right)$. Hence, we need to show that a net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E$ is compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ if and only if it is compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]$. In fact, arguing as in (ii) we have that $e_{\alpha}=f^{*}_{\alpha}+e_{\alpha}\left(0_{F}\right)\1$, where $e_{\alpha}\left(0_{F}\right)\to 0$, and $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is compact-open-null (in either sense). Note that the $f_{\alpha}^{*}$'s when represented as functions on $\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]$ only depend on the first variable. Hence, if $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]$, then it is clearly compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. Conversely, suppose $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. If $K\subseteq \mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]$ is compact, there is a compact $L\subseteq F$ such that $K\subseteq L\times\left[-1,1\right]$. Using this, one can show that $\left(f^{*}_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is compact-open-null on $\mathrm{B}_{F}\times \left[-1,1\right]$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- proposition-40: body_md -->
\label{ouoc}
Let $\left(E,e\right)$ be an order unit space, embedded into $\mathcal{C}\left(\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}K_{E},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$ via $f\mapsto \hat{f}$ as described prior to Theorem~\ref{T:rep of o.u.s.}. Then:
\item[(i)] Order convergence in $E$ is the restriction of order convergence in $\mathcal{C}\left(\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}K_{E},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.
\item[(ii)] Weak convergence implies order convergence for sequences in $E$.
\item[(iii)] If additionally $E^{*}$ is separable, then bounded weak convergence is stronger than order convergence in $E$.
<!-- end proposition-40 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Denote $K:=\left(\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}K_{E},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.

(i) follows from the fact that $E$ is supremum-dense in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ and Proposition~\ref{ocp}.

(ii): Assume that $e_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{w}} 0_{E}$. First, it follows from the Banach--Steinhaus theorem (see \cite[Theorem~3.85]{fhhmz}) that $\left\{e_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is norm bounded, and therefore also order bounded. Next, by definition we see that $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges to $\0$ pointwise in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$. According to the comment before the proposition, this implies $e_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} \0$ in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$, and so by (i) we conclude that $e_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{o}} 0_{E}$ in $E$.

(iii): First, $E$ is separable, and so $\left(\mathrm{B}_{E^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$ is metrizable; it also follows that $\left(\mathrm{B}_{E},\mathrm{w}\right)$ is metrizable (for these results see \cite[Propositions~2.8, 3.103 and~3.105]{fhhmz}). In particular, $K$ is metrizable and compact, and so order convergence in $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ is strongly first countable (see \cite[discussion after Proposition~4.21]{bbv}). Furthermore, $\left(\mathrm{B}_{E},\mathrm{w}\right)$ is metrizable, thus also strongly first countable. By (ii), the embedding of $\left(\mathrm{B}_{E},\mathrm{w}\right)$ into $\left(\mathcal{C}\left(K\right),\mathrm{o}\right)$ is sequentially continuous, and so it is in fact continuous by \cite[Theorem~5.2]{bbv}. Thus, using (i) again we conclude that bounded weak convergence is stronger than order convergence in $E$.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{densenet}
Assume that the weak and $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topologies agree on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$. Furthermore, let $E:= \operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$.
If a net $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq \mathrm{B}_{E}$ converges to $\0$ pointwise on a $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-dense subset of $\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$, then it converges weakly in $E$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Let $C:=\left\{\nu\in \mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}: e_{\alpha}\left(\nu\right)\to 0\right\}$. By part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{iceo}, it is enough to show that $C=\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. Since every $e_{\alpha}$ is affine, $C$ is convex. Let us show that $C$ is norm-closed. Assume that $\mu$ is in the norm closure of $C$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. There is $\nu\in C$ such that $\|\mu-\nu\|\le\varepsilon$. Find $\alpha_{0}$ such that $\left|e_{\alpha}\left(\nu\right)\right|\le\varepsilon$, for all $\alpha\ge \alpha_{0}$. For $\alpha\ge \alpha_{0}$ we have that $e_{\alpha}=f_{\alpha}+r_{\alpha}\1$, where $r_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $f_{\alpha}\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$, hence
\[\left|e_{\alpha}\left(\mu\right)\right|=\left|f_{\alpha}\left(\mu\right)+r_{\alpha}\right|\le \left|f_{\alpha}\left(\nu\right)+r_{\alpha}\right|+\left|f_{\alpha}\left(\mu-\nu\right)\right|=\left|e_{\alpha}\left(\nu\right)\right|+\left|f_{\alpha}\left(\mu-\nu\right)\right|
\le2\varepsilon.\]
Thus, $\mu\in C$. Being a norm-closed convex set, $C$ is weakly closed. By assumption, $C\cap \mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-dense in $\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. Let us show that $C$ is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-dense in $\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. Since $C$ is convex, so is $D:=\overline{C}$. We have that $D\supseteq \overline{C\cap \mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}}\supseteq \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$, hence by the Krein--Milman theorem, we conclude that $D\supseteq \overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left( \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}\right)=\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$.

Let $\mu\in\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$. As $C$ is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-dense, there is $\left(\nu_{\beta}\right)_{\beta\in B}\subseteq C$ such that $\nu_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{{\mathrm{w}^{*}}}\mu$. Then, $1=\|\mu\|\le\liminf_{\beta\in B}\|\nu_{\beta}\|\le\limsup_{\beta\in B}\|\nu_{\beta}\|\le 1$ implies $\|\nu_{\beta}\|\to 1$, and so without loss of generality we assume $\nu_{\beta}\ne 0_{F^{*}}$, for every $\beta$. It follows that $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}\ni\mu_{\beta}:=\|\nu_{\beta}\|^{-1}\nu_{\beta}\to\mu$ in the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology, and so by our assumption we get $\mu_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{w}}\mu$. Therefore, $\nu_{\beta}=\|\nu_{\beta}\|\mu_{\beta}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{w}}\mu$, and since $\nu_{\beta}\in C$ and $C$ is weakly closed, we conclude that $\mu\in C$. Thus, $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}\subseteq C$, hence $\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}=\operatorname{conv}\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}\subseteq C$, as required.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proposition-41: body_md -->
\label{iceor}
\item[(i)] Weak convergence implies order convergence for sequences in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$.
\item[(ii)] If, additionally, $F^{*}$ is separable, then bounded weak convergence is stronger than order convergence in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$.
\item[(iii)] If, additionally, weak and $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-convergences agree on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$, then order convergence is stronger than bounded weak convergence in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$.
<!-- end proposition-41 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
(i) follows immediately from part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{ouoc}. (ii) follows from part~(iii) of Proposition~\ref{ouoc} and the fact that $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)^{*}\simeq F^{*}\oplus_{\8} \mathbb{R}$.

(iii): Assume that $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq E:= 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is order-null. By part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{ouoc} and the discussion preceding it, there are $\alpha_{0}$ and $r>0$ such that the net $\left(re_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}$ is contained in $\mathrm{B}_{E}$ and converges pointwise on a co-meager set in $\left(\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)$. The latter is a compact Hausdorff space, and so any co-meager subset of this space is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-dense. By Lemma~\ref{densenet}, the net $\left(re_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\ge\alpha_{0}}$ is weakly null. Thus, $\left(e_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is bounded weakly null.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{iceord}
Assume that $F^{*}$ is separable and that the weak and $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topologies agree on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$. Let $E:=\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right)\simeq  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$. Then:
\item[(i)] Order, bounded weak and bounded pointwise convergences agree on $E$.
\item[(ii)] Order intervals in $E$ are order metrizable and order pre-compact.
\item[(iii)] $\dim F=\8$ if and only if directed order convergence is strictly stronger than order convergence in $E$.
\item[(iv)] Order intervals in $E$ are order compact if and only if $E$ is order complete if and only if $F$ is reflexive.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
(i) follows from combining parts~(ii) and (iii) of Proposition~\ref{iceor} and part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{iceo}. (ii) follows from the facts that balls in $E$ are metrizable and pre-compact in the weak topology, that order and weak convergences agree on balls, and that every order interval in $E$ is norm bounded. (iii) follows from (i) and part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{icedo}.

(iv): If $F$ is reflexive, then so is $E$, and so order intervals in $E$ are weakly compact, which by (i) is equivalent to order compact.

If order intervals are order compact, then they are order complete. Since every order Cauchy net has a tail contained in an order interval, it follows that $E$ is order complete.

We now assume that $F$ is not reflexive and show that $E$ is not order complete. As $E$ is also not reflexive, we have that $\mathrm{B}_{E^{**}}\setminus\mathrm{B}_{E}\ne\varnothing$. By Goldstine's theorem, there is a net in $\mathrm{B}_{E}$ which $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-converges to $g\in \mathrm{B}_{E^{**}}\setminus\mathrm{B}_{E}$, and so it is a weakly Cauchy net, which does not have a weak limit. By (i), this net is also order Cauchy but not order convergent, thus showing that $E$ is not order complete.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{iceord2}
Let $F$ be a separable reflexive Banach space. Then, on $\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\|\cdot\|\right)$ order convergence coincides with continuous convergence, while the order topology coincides with the compact-open topology.
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
First, note that the weak and $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topologies agree on $F^{*}$, and so
\[E:=\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\|\cdot\|\right)=\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}\right)=\operatorname{Aff}\left(\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}},\mathrm{w}^{*}\right).\] Since $F$ is separable and reflexive, it follows that $F^{*}$ is separable.                                                                                                           
Thus, $F$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{iceord}, and so order convergence, bounded weak convergence and bounded pointwise convergence all agree on $E$. By part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{iceo}, bounded pointwise convergence also agrees with continuous convergence in $E$. As $E\simeq F\oplus_{1}\mathbb{R}$ is reflexive, bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-convergence coincides with bounded weak convergence, and hence with order convergence. The compact-open topology is equal to the bounded $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology by part~(iii) of Proposition~\ref{iceo}, and so it is equal to the order topology.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
\label{iceord1}
Let $F$ be a non-reflexive Banach space such that $F^{*}$ is separable and locally uniformly rotund. Then, $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is directed order complete, but not order complete.
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
First, $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is directed order complete by part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{icedo}. As $F^{*}$ is LUR, it is strictly convex and has the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-Kadec--Klee property, i.e.\ every $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-convergent sequence in $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ is norm-convergent (see \cite[Exercise~8.45]{fhhmz}). Since $F$ is separable, the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ is metrizable. We have two metrizable topologies on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$, which agree on sequences, hence these topologies coincide. As the weak topology is stronger than the $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-topology but weaker than the norm topology, it follows that all three topologies coincide on $\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$. Hence, $F$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{iceord}, and since it is not reflexive, by part~(iv) of that theorem, $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is not order complete.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{iceable}
Let $0_{F}\ne f\in F$. There is an ordered vector space structure on $F$ such that $f$ is an order unit with respect to this order and the order unit norm on $F$ agrees with the original norm if and only if $\nu\left(f\right)=\pm 1$, for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. In this case, $\|f\|=1$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Necessity: According to \cite[Definition~1.10 and Theorem~1.19]{as2}, we have that $\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}=\operatorname{conv}\left(K_{F}\cup-K_{F}\right)$, where $K_{F}$ is the set of states on $\left(F,f\right)$. Then, any extreme point of $\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ has to be contained in either $K_{F}$ or $-K_{F}$ and be extreme there. Thus, for every $\nu\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ either $\nu$ or $-\nu$ is a pure state on $\left(F,f\right)$, and so in particular, $\nu\left(f\right)=\pm 1$.

Sufficiency: Let $K:=\left\{\nu\in \mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}: \nu\left(f\right)=1\right\}$, which is $\mathrm{w}^{*}$-compact. By assumption, $\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}\subseteq K\cup -K$, and so by the Krein--Milman theorem, we have that
\[\|h\|=\bigvee_{\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}}\left|\nu\left(h\right)\right|=\bigvee_{\nu\in K}\left|\nu\left(h\right)\right|,\quad\text{for every }h\in F.\]
Let $J\colon F\to\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ be defined by $\left[Jh\right]\left(\nu\right):=\nu\left(h\right)$. Then, $Jf=\1$, and by the preceding step, $J$ is an isometry, and so we may view $F$ as a subspace of $\mathcal{C}\left(K\right)$ with $\1=f\in F$. Hence, the norm on $F$ is the order unit norm of $\left(F,f\right)$.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- proposition-42: body_md -->
\label{antilattice}
For $f,g\in F$ and $r,s\in\mathbb{R}$ we have that $\left(f,r\right)\wedge \left(g,s\right)=0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}$ if and only if one of the following conditions is satisfied:
\begin{itemize}
\item $f=0_{F}$, $r=0$ and $\|g\|\le s$;
\item $g=0_{F}$, $s=0$ and $\|f\|\le r$;
\item $r,s>0$, $sf+rg=0_{F}$, and $\frac{1}{r}f=-\frac{1}{s}g$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma~\ref{iceable} (in particular, $\|f\|=r$ and $\|g\|=s$).
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-42 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Necessity: First, it follows that $\left(f,r\right), \left(g,s\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$, and so $\|f\|\le r$ and $\|g\|\le s$. In particular, if $r=0$, then $f=0_{F}$, and if $s=0$, then $g=0_{F}$. Hence, we may assume from now on that $r,s>0$.

It follows from the discussion before the proposition that $\left(f,r\right)\wedge \left(g,s\right)=0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}$ if and only if $\left<\left(f,r\right),\left(\nu,1\right)\right>\left<\left(g,s\right),\left(\nu,1\right)\right>=0$, for every $\nu\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. This is equivalent to either $\nu\left(f\right)=-r$, or $\nu\left(g\right)=-s$, for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. Note that if for some $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ we have $\nu\left(f\right)=-r$, then $-\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$, and $-\nu\left(f\right)=r\ne -r$, and so $-\nu\left(g\right)=-s$, or $\nu\left(g\right)=s$. Conversely, if $\nu\left(g\right)=-s$, then $\nu\left(f\right)=r$, and so $\nu\left(sf+rg\right)=0$ for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$. By the Krein--Milman theorem, it follows that $sf+rg=0_{F}$. It is also clear that for $h:=\frac{1}{r}f$ we have $\nu\left(h\right)=\pm 1$, for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$.

Sufficiency of the first two conditions is clear. The third case can be obtained by reversing the arguments in the previous paragraph.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- corollary-19: body_md -->
If $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is weakly pervasive, then $\dim F\le 1$, in which case it is a vector lattice.
<!-- end corollary-19 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
It is clear that $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is a vector lattice if $\dim F=0$. If $\dim F= 1$, one can show that the clockwise rotation by $\frac{\pi}{4}$ is an order isomorphism between $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ and $\mathbb{R}^{2}$, which is a vector lattice.

Assume that $\dim F> 1$, so that there are linearly independent $\nu,\mu\in \operatorname{ext} \mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ (this follows from the Krein--Milman theorem). Find $f\in\mathrm{S}_{F}$ such that $\mu\left(f\right)=0\ne \nu\left(f\right)$. Then, $f$ does not satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{iceable}, and so according to Proposition~\ref{antilattice}, the infimum of $\left(f,1\right)$ and $\left(-f,1\right)$ does not exist. On the other hand, let us show that $\left(f,1\right)\wedge_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}}\left(-f,1\right)=\left(0_{F},0\right)$, which will prove that $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is not weakly pervasive. Indeed, if $0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}\le \left(g,r\right)\le \left(\pm f,1\right)$, then $\|f-g\|,\|f+g\|\le 1-r$, hence
\[2=\|2f\|\le \|f-g\|+\|f+g\|\le 2-2r,\]
which yields $r=0$ and $g=0_{F}$.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- proposition-43: body_md -->
For $f,g\in F$ and $r,s\in\mathbb{R}$ we have that $\left(f,r\right)\perp \left(g,s\right)$ if and only if one of the following conditions is satisfied:
\begin{itemize}
\item $f=0_{F}$, $r=0$;
\item $g=0_{F}$, $s=0$;
\item $r,s\ne 0$, $sf+rg=0_{F}$, and $\frac{1}{r}f=-\frac{1}{s}g$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma~\ref{iceable} (in particular, $\|f\|=\left|r\right|$ and $\|g\|=\left|s\right|$);
\item $r=s=0$ and $\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}\subseteq f^{\top}\cup g^{\top}$.\footnote{In order to distinguish from the disjoint complement, we denote the annihilator of $A\subseteq F$ by $A^{\top}$.}
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-43 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Arguing as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{antilattice}, one can show that $\left(f,r\right)\perp \left(g,s\right)$ if and only if either $\nu\left(f\right)=-r$, or $\nu\left(g\right)=-s$, for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$.

Moreover, if $r,s\ne 0$, we are in a similar situation as in that proposition.

Assume that $r\ne 0$ and $s=0$. If $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ satisfies $\nu\left(f\right)=-r$, then $-\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ and $-\nu\left(f\right)=r\ne -r$, and so $-\nu\left(g\right)=0$, or $\nu\left(g\right)=0$. If $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ is such that $\nu\left(f\right)\ne-r$, then also $\nu\left(g\right)=0$. Hence, $g=0_{F}$.

Similarly, if $r= 0$ and $s\ne 0$, we obtain that $f=0_{F}$.

If $r=s=0$, it follows that for every $\nu\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ either $\nu\left(f\right)=0$ or $\nu\left(g\right)=0$, so that $\nu\in f^{\top}\cup g^{\top}$.

Sufficiency of the third condition is proved using the arguments from the proof of Proposition~\ref{antilattice}; sufficiency of the other conditions is clear.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- corollary-20: body_md -->
\label{antilattice2}
If $\dim F>1$ and $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, then $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is disjointness-free. Moreover, whenever $P\subseteq  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is a finite set such that $\bigvee P$ exists, then this supremum is in fact the maximum, i.e.\ there is $p\in P$ such that $\bigvee P=p$.
<!-- end corollary-20 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
For the first claim, note that if $\dim F>1$ and $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, then no elements of $F$ satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{iceable}, and the extreme points of $\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ cannot be covered by two hyperplanes.

In order to prove the second claim, assume that $\left(f_{1},r_{1}\right),\ldots,\left(f_{n},r_{n}\right)\in  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ are such that $\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\left(f_{k},r_{k}\right)=0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}$. By the comment before Proposition~\ref{antilattice}, it follows that for every $\nu\in \mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ we have
\[\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\left<\left(f_{k},r_{k}\right),\left(\nu,1\right)\right>=\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\left(\nu\left(f_{k}\right)+r_{k}\right)=0.\] Since $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, for every $f\in F$ there is a unique $\nu_{f}\in \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ with $\nu_{f}\left(f\right)=-\|f\|$ (combine \cite[Corollaries~7.23(i) and~7.22(ii)]{fhhmz}); in particular, if $\nu_{f}\ne \nu\in\mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$, then $\|f\|>-\nu\left(f\right)$. Since $\dim F>1$ and $F^{*}$ is strictly convex, we have that $\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}\supseteq \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ is infinite. Hence, we can select $\nu\in \mathrm{S}_{F^{*}}$ such that $\nu\ne\nu_{f_{k}}$, for $k=1,\ldots,n$. Then, for every $k=1,\ldots,n$ we have that $\left(f_{k},r_{k}\right)\ge 0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}$, thus $r_{k}\ge \|f_{k}\|>-\nu\left(f_{k}\right)$. This implies $\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n}\left(\nu\left(f_{k}\right)+r_{k}\right)>0$, contradiction.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
In the case when $\dim F=\8$, the proof of the last claim in Corollary~\ref{antilattice2} is simplified: for every $\nu\in \mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}=\mathrm{B}_{F^{*}}$ we have $\bigwedge_{\left(f,r\right)\in P}\left<\left(f,r\right),\left(\nu,1\right)\right>=0$, and so taking $\nu=0_{F^{*}}$ yields $\bigwedge_{\left(f,r\right)\in P}r=0$. Hence, there is $\left(f,0\right)\in P$. Since $P\subseteq

\left(F\right)_{+}$, it follows that $f=0_{F}$.
