<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\label{watom}
Let $F:=\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]\oplus c$, and let $E:=\left\{f\oplus g\in F: \int f=\lim_{\8} g\right\}$. Then, $E$ is Archimedean, and it is also directed, since it has an order unit. Let us show that $E$ is atomic. Let $\left\{e_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be the standard basis of $c_{00}\subseteq c$. Clearly, $\0\oplus e_{n}$ is an atom in $E$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $f\oplus g>\0\oplus\0$. Then, either $g>\0$, or $f>\0$, but in the latter case, $\lim_{\8} g=\int f>0$, and so $g>\0$. Hence, there is $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $g\left(n\right)>0$, thus $g\ge g\left(n\right)\left(\0\oplus e_{n}\right)$.

Let us show that $\1\oplus\1$ is not a supremum of a collection of atoms. To this end, note that the atoms in $\left[\0\oplus\0,\1\oplus\1\right]$ are of the form $\0\oplus re_{n}$, $r\in\left(0,1\right]$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $P$ be the set of these atoms. Then, $P^{\uparrow}=\left\{f\oplus g\in E_{+}: g\ge\1\right\}$. It is easy to see that $P^{\uparrow}$ does not have a least element, and so $P$ does not have a supremum.

Let us show that the interval $\left[\0\oplus\0,\1\oplus\1\right]$ is not order pre-compact. We construct a net $\left(f_{\gamma}\right)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ in $\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]$ as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{pervnoc}, taking $Z:=\mathbb{Q}$. For every $\gamma\in\Gamma$ let $g_{\gamma}:=\left(\int f_{\gamma}\right)\1$. Using the same arguments one can show that if $f\oplus g$ is an eventual upper (resp. lower) bound of any subnet of the net $\left(f_{\gamma}\oplus g_{\gamma}\right)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$, then $f\ge\1$ (resp. $f\le\0$). Consequently, no subnet of this net is order Cauchy. Starting with the net constructed in the proof of (iv)$\Rightarrow$(v) in Theorem~\ref{ordprec}, and selecting a subnet such that $\int f_{\gamma}\to r$, for some $r\in\left[0,1\right]$, shows that order convergence in $\left[\0\oplus\0,\1\oplus\1\right]$ does not have the Choquet property, hence is not topological.
\qed
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Does directed order compactness of order intervals imply existence of an atom?
\qed
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{corresp}
There is an order isomorphism between the collection of faces of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and the collection of nonempty faces of $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$. It is given by
\[A\mapsto C_{A}:=\left\{r\left(f,1\right): f\in A,~r>0\right\}\cup\left\{0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}\right\},\]
and its inverse is given by $C\mapsto A_{C}:=\left\{f\in\mathrm{B}_{F}:\left(f,1\right)\in C\right\}$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
It is easy to see that if $C$ is a nonempty face of $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$, then $A_{C}$ is a face of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$.

Suppose now that $A\subseteq\mathrm{B}_{F}$ is a face. We will deduce from Proposition~\ref{face} that $C_{A}$ is a nonempty face of $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$. Indeed, if $g,h\in F$, $s\ge\|g\|$, and $t\ge\|h\|$ are such that $\left(g,s\right)+\left(h,t\right)\in C_{A}$, then $A\ni\frac{1}{s+t}\left(g+h\right)=\frac{s}{s+t}\frac{g}{s}+\frac{t}{s+t}\frac{h}{t}$ implies that $\frac{g}{s}\in A$, and thus $\left(g,s\right)=s\left(\frac{g}{s},1\right)\in C_{A}$ (we leave the case when $s$ or $t$ is $0$ to the reader).

It is also straightforward to check that the introduced correspondences are mutually inverse and order preserving.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{ineq}
Let $f,g\in F$ and $t\in\left[0,1\right]$. Then, $\left(f,1\right)\ge t\left(g,1\right)$ if and only if there is $h\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
The case $t=1$ is trivial, and so we assume that $t<1$. If $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$, for some $h\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$, then $\|f-tg\|=\left(1-t\right)\|h\|\le 1-t$, and so $\left(f-tg,1-t\right)\ge 0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}$. Conversely, if $\left(f,1\right)\ge t\left(g,1\right)$, then $\|f-tg\|\le 1-t$, or $h:=\frac{f-tg}{1-t}\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$; we then have $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- corollary-21: body_md -->
\label{atom}
Atoms in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ are of the form $r\left(g,1\right)$, where $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$, and $r>0$.
<!-- end corollary-21 -->
<!-- proposition-44: body_md -->
\label{atm}The following conditions are equivalent:
\item[(i)] $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is atomic;
\item[(ii)] Every nonempty face of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ contains an extreme point;
\item[(iii)] Every $f\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ can be written as $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$, where $t\in\left(0,1\right]$, $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$;
\item[(iv)] Every $f\in \mathrm{S}_{F}$ can be written as $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$, where $t\in\left(0,1\right]$, $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$.\medskip

In particular, if $\dim F<\8$, then $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is atomic.
<!-- end proposition-44 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii): The order isomorphism between the collection of faces of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and the collection of nonempty faces of $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$ considered in Lemma~\ref{corresp} sets extreme points of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$ in correspondence with extreme rays of $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$. Hence, the equivalence follows from part~(ii) of Corollary~\ref{atmo}.

(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii): According to Corollary~\ref{atom}, $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is atomic if and only if for every $f\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$ there are $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $t>0$ such that $\left(f,1\right)\ge t\left(g,1\right)$, which by Lemma~\ref{ineq} is equivalent to $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$, for some $h\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$.

(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv) is trivial. To get the converse, we may assume that $r:=\|f\|\in\left(0,1\right)$, and find $t\in\left(0,1\right]$, $h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $\frac{1}{r}f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$. Then, $f=rtg+r\left(1-t\right)h=rtg+\left(1-rt\right)e$, where $e=\frac{r\left(1-t\right)}{1-rt}h$. As $r\left(1-t\right)\le 1-rt$, we conclude that $e\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$.

The last claim follows from (ii), the Krein--Milman theorem and the fact that every face of a convex set in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is closed (see \cite[Corollary~18.1.1]{rockafellar}).
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
It was proved in \cite[Theorem~1]{als} that if $F$ is a Banach space, then the conditions of Proposition~\ref{atm} are also equivalent to the fact that for every $f\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ there are $\left(t_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\left[0,1\right]$ and $\left(g_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}t_{n}=1$ and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}t_{n}g_{n}=f$. Note that this property is strictly weaker than the Krein--Milman property (see \cite[Remark~3.4]{als}).
\qed
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{smoothre}
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\ge 1$ let $\mathrm{B}_{p}^{n}$ be the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with respect to the $\ell_{p}$-norm. Let $u_{n}:=\left(\frac{1}{n},\dots,\frac{1}{n}\right)\in\mathrm{B}_{1}^{n}\cap \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathrm{B}_{2}^{n}$.

Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $F_{n}$ be $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ endowed with the norm whose unit ball is $\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}:=\mathrm{B}_{1}^{n}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathrm{B}_{2}^{n}$, which is a compact convex body. If $f\in\partial\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}$, then it must be on the $\ell_{2}$-sphere centered at some $e\in \partial\mathrm{B}_{1}^{n}$ of radius $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. Any supporting hyperplane to $\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}$ through $f$ cannot intersect this sphere in any other point, which means that it is the tangent hyperplane to the sphere, ensuring its uniqueness. Hence, the support hyperplane to $\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}$ is unique at each boundary point, and so $F_{n}$ is a smooth normed space. Then, $F_{n}^{*}$ is strictly convex, hence LUR (combine reflexivity of $F_{n}$, \cite[Corollary~7.23(ii), Exercise~9.1 and Fact~9.5]{fhhmz}).

Let $\nu_{n}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the linear functional defined by $\nu_{n}\left(r_{1},\dots,r_{n}\right):=r_{1}+\dots+r_{n}$. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, the maximal value of $\nu_{n}$ on $\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}$ is $2$, and so
\[A_{n}:=\nu_{n}^{-1}\left(2\right)\cap \mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}=u_{n}+\left\{\left(r_{1},\dots,r_{n}\right): r_{1},\dots,r_{n}\ge 0,~ r_{1}+\dots+r_{n}=1\right\}\]
is a face of $\mathrm{B}_{F_{n}}$. The extreme points of $A_{n}$ are of the form $u_{n}+e_{k}^{n}$, $k=1,\dots,n$, where $e_{1}^{n},\dots,e_{n}^{n}$ is the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. It follows that if $f\in\operatorname{ext} A_{n}$, then $\|f\|_{\ell_{\8}}=1+\frac{1}{n}$. Also, note that $\|u_{n}\|_{\ell_{\8}}=\frac{1}{n}$ and $2u_{n}\in A_{n}$.

Let $F$ be the $\ell_{2}$-sum of the $F_{n}$'s, over $n\in\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $F$ is reflexive and separable, and moreover $F^{*}$ is LUR (combine \cite[Exercises~2.32 and~8.4]{fhhmz}). Fix any $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \in \mathrm{S}_{\ell_{2}}$ with $a_{n} > 0$ for all $n$. Define
$A:= \left\{\left(a_{n}f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \in F: \forall n, f_{n}\in A_{n}\right\}$ and $A':=\left\{\left(a_{n}f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \in A: \|f_{n}\|_{\ell_{\8}}\to 0\right\}$.

It is clear that $A$ is a convex subset of $\mathrm{S}_{F}$. Let us show that it is a face of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. Assume that $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, \left(h_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\mathrm{S}_{F}$ and $t\in\left(0,1\right)$ are such that $\left(te_{n}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in A$. Then, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $f_{n}\in A_{n}$ such that $te_{n}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n}=a_{n}f_{n}$. We have that
\begin{align*}
1&=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left\|te_{n}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n}\right\|^{2}_{F_{n}}\le \sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left(t\|e_{n}\|_{F_{n}}+\left(1-t\right)\|h_{n}\|_{F_{n}}\right)^{2} \\
&\le t\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|e_{n}\|^{2}_{F_{n}}+\left(1-t\right)\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|h_{n}\|^{2}_{F_{n}}=t+1-t=1.
\end{align*}
Hence, both inequalities in the above formula are in fact equalities. Due to strict convexity of the $\ell_{2}$-norm, the second of these equalities yields $\left(\|e_{n}\|\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}=\left(\|h_{n}\|\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. Therefore, the first equality now becomes $a_{n}=\|a_{n}f_{n}\|=\left\|te_{n}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n}\right\|=\|e_{n}\|=\|h_{n}\|$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. It follows that $\frac{1}{a_{n}}e_{n},\frac{1}{a_{n}}h_{n}\in\mathrm{S}_{F_{n}}$ satisfy $\frac{t}{a_{n}}e_{n}+\frac{1-t}{a_{n}}h_{n}\in A_{n}$, which implies $\frac{1}{a_{n}}e_{n},\frac{1}{a_{n}}h_{n}\in A_{n}$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. We conclude that $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, \left(h_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in A$.

It is also clear that $A'$ is convex, and it is nonempty as $\left(2a_{n}u_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in A'$. Let us show that it is a face of $A$, and hence a face of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. Suppose that $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in A\setminus A'$, $\left(h_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in A$ and $t\in\left(0,1\right)$. There are $\varepsilon>0$ and an increasing sequence $\left(n_{k}\right)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $\|e_{n_{k}}\|_{\ell_{\8}}\ge\varepsilon$, for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, $te_{n_{k}}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n_{k}}\ge te_{n_{k}}$, hence
\[\left\|te_{n_{k}}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n_{k}}\right\|_{\ell_{\8}}\ge \|te_{n_{k}}\|_{\ell_{\8}}\ge t\varepsilon,\quad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb{N}.\] Thus, $\lim_{k \to \infty}\left\|te_{n_{k}}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n_{k}}\right\|_{\ell_{\8}}\ne 0$, and therefore $\left(te_{n}+\left(1-t\right)h_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\notin A'$.

To show that $A'$ has no extreme points, it is enough to prove that all extreme points of $A$ lie outside of $A'$. We have $\operatorname{ext} A= \left\{\left(a_{n}f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \in F: \forall n, f_{n}\in \operatorname{ext} A_{n}\right\}$. As $f_{n}\in \operatorname{ext} A_{n}$ implies $\|f_{n}\|=1+\frac{1}{n}\not\to 0$, we conclude that $\operatorname{ext} A\cap A'=\varnothing$.
\qed
<!-- end example-11 -->

<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Let $f\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $P:=\left[0_{ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-0.7ex,scale=0.08]{
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)}, (f,1)\right]\cap \partial  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$. It is enough to show that every upper bound $\left(e,r\right)$ of $P$ satisfies $\left(e,r\right) \ge \left(f,1\right)$.

First, assume that $e\ne f$. For the continuous function $v\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by
\[v\left(s\right):=s\|f-e\|+\left\|f+s\left(f-e\right)\right\|,\]
we have $v\left(0\right)=\|f\|\le 1$, and $\lim_{s\to+\8}v\left(s\right)=+\8$, hence there is $s_{0}\ge 0$ such that $v\left(s_{0}\right)=1$.

Let $g:=f+s_{0}\left(f-e\right)$; we have $\|g\|=1-s_{0}\|f-e\|$ and $f-g=s_{0}\left(e-f\right)$, which yields $\left(g,\|g\|\right)\le\left(f,1\right)$, so that $\left(g,\|g\|\right)\in P$. It follows that $\left(g,\|g\|\right)\le \left(e,r\right)$, hence
$\left(1+s_{0}\right)\left\|e-f\right\|=\|e-g\|\le r-\|g\|=r-1+s_{0}\|f-e\|$, and so $\left\|e-f\right\|\le r-1$, i.e.\ $\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(f,1\right)$.

If $e=f\ne 0_{F}$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have that $\left(1+\varepsilon\right)\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(e,r\right)\ge P$, and so by the preceding case we have $\left(1+\varepsilon\right)\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(f,1\right)$. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(f,1\right)$. Finally, if $e=f=0_{F}$, take $h\in\mathrm{S}_{F}$. Then, $\bigl(\frac{1}{2}h,\frac{1}{2}\bigr)\in P$ is dominated by $\left(0_{F},r\right)$, which implies $r-\frac{1}{2}\ge \left\|\frac{1}{2}h\right\|=\frac{1}{2}$, and so $r\ge 1$. Thus, $\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(0_{F},1\right)=\left(f,1\right)$.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{stratm}
\item[(i)] If $f\in \mathrm{S}_{F}$, then $\left(f,1\right)$ is strongly atomic in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ if and only if for every $t\in\left[0,1\right)$ there are $g,h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$.
\item[(ii)] $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is strongly atomic if and only if for every $f\in \mathrm{S}_{F}$ and $t\in\left[0,1\right)$ there are $g,h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
(i): Let $P$ be the collection of all atoms beneath $\left(f,1\right)$.

Necessity: Let $t\in\left[0,1\right)$. We have $\left(0_{F},2t\right)\not\ge\left(f,1\right)$, since $\|0_{F}-f\|=1>2t-1$. As $\left(f,1\right)=\bigvee P$, it follows that $\left(0_{F},2t\right)$ is not an upper bound for $P$. Hence, there is an atom $e\in P$ such that $\left(0_{F},2t\right)\not\ge e$. By Corollary~\ref{atom}, there are $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $r>0$ such that $e=r\left(g,1\right)$. The condition $\left(0_{F},2t\right)\not\ge r\left(g,1\right)$ implies $r=\|0_{F}-rg\|>2t-r$, therefore $r>t$. It follows that $\left(f,1\right)\ge r\left(g,1\right)\ge t \left(g,1\right)$, which by Lemma~\ref{ineq} yields $f=tg+\left(1-t\right)h$, for some $h\in\mathrm{B}_{F}$.

Sufficiency: Let $\left(e,r\right)$ be an upper bound for $P$. Fix $\varepsilon\in\left(0,1\right)$. There are $g\in\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ and $h\in \mathrm{B}_{F}$ such that $f=\left(1-\varepsilon\right)g+\varepsilon h$. For $u:=\left(1-\varepsilon\right)g$, we have $\|f-u\|=\varepsilon\|h\|\le\varepsilon$, and so $\left(f,1\right)\ge \left(u,1-\varepsilon\right)$. By Corollary~\ref{atom}, the latter vector is an atom, therefore contained in $P$, and so by our assumption, $\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(u,1-\varepsilon\right)$, i.e.\ $\|e-u\|\le r-1+\varepsilon$. Hence,
\[\|e-f\|\le \|f-u\|+\|e-u\|\le \varepsilon+r-1+\varepsilon=r-1+2\varepsilon.\] As $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $\|e-f\|\le r-1$, thus $\left(e,r\right)\ge\left(f,1\right)$. This justifies that $\left(f,1\right)=\bigvee P$.

(ii): Necessity follows immediately from (i). For sufficiency, first note that (i) guarantees that every vector in $\partial  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)_{+}$ is strongly atomic, and then use Proposition~\ref{iceprop} and the fact that the collection of strongly atomic vectors is closed under taking suprema.

<!-- proposition-46: body_md -->
\label{strictstrong}
\item[(i)] If $F$ is strictly convex, then $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is strongly atomic. The converse holds if $\dim F<\8$.
\item[(ii)] If $\dim F<\8$ and $f\in \mathrm{S}_{F}$, then $\left(f,1\right)$ is strongly atomic if and only if it is an atom if and only if $f\in \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$.
<!-- end proposition-46 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
The first claim in (i) follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{stratm}, while the second claim follows from (ii).

(ii): The second equivalence was established in Corollary~\ref{atom}. It is also clear that every atom is strongly atomic. Suppose that $\left(f,1\right)$ is strongly atomic. According to \cite[Theorem~2.10]{al}, if $f\in\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F}\setminus \operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$, then the criterion in part~(i) of Theorem~\ref{stratm} is not satisfied, contradiction. It is also clear that if $f\notin\mathop{\overline{\operatorname{ext}}}\mathrm{B}_{F}$, the criterion in part~(i) of Theorem~\ref{stratm} is not satisfied either. We conclude that $f$ is extreme.
<!-- end proof-71 -->

If $F$ and $F^{*}$ are strictly convex with $\dim F=\8$ (e.g., if $F=\ell_{2}$), then $

<!-- example-14: body_md -->
\label{ellipse}
  Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by
\[f\left(x,y\right):=\sqrt{(x - 1)^2 + y^2} + \sqrt{(x + 1)^2 +y^2}.\]
Clearly, $f$ is a symmetric convex function, therefore $B:=\left\{\left(x,y,z\right): \left|z\right|+f\left(x,y\right) \le 4\right\}$ is a symmetric convex body; see the figure below.
                 
\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[scale=0.4 ]{ball_dutch_paper.jpg}
    \label{fig:placeholder}
\end{figure}
              
Moreover, when $y\ne 0$, we have that
\[
\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}\left(x,y\right)=\frac{y^2}{((x - 1)^2 + y^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}+\frac{y^2}{((x + 1)^2 + y^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}>0
\]
and the determinant of the Hessian matrix of $f$ is
\[
\frac{4 y^2}{\left(\left((x -1)^2 + y^2\right)\left((x+1)^2 + y^2\right)\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}>0,
\]
implying that $f$ is strictly convex when $y\ne0$. It follows that all points on the boundary $\partial B= \left\{\left(x,y,z\right): \left|z\right|=4-f\left(x,y\right)\right\}$ with $y\ne 0$ are extreme points of $B$. Note that $B$ is not strictly convex, as $\partial B$ contains $\left\{\left(x,y,z\right): y=0,~ \left|z\right|+\left|x+1\right|+\left|x-1\right|=4\right\}$, which is a broken line. Now let $F$ be $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with the norm given by the Minkowski functional of $B$. Then, $\mathrm{B}_{F}=B$, and so $\operatorname{ext}\mathrm{B}_{F}$ is dense in $\mathrm{S}_{F}$. However, $\mathrm{B}_{F}=B$ is not strictly convex, and so by part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{strictstrong}, $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is not strongly atomic.
\qed
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
The sum of two atoms may fail to be a strongly atomic element. Indeed, let $F:=\ell_{\8}^{2}$, and let $f:=\left(1,1\right)$ and $g:=\left(1,-1\right)$. Note that $\frac{1}{2}\left(f+g\right)\in \mathrm{S}_{F}$ is not an extreme point of $\mathrm{B}_{F}$. Then, $e:=\left(f,1\right)$ and $h:=\left(g,1\right)$ are atoms in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$, but $\frac{1}{2}\left(e+h\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(f+g\right),1\right)$ is not strongly atomic, according to part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{strictstrong}.

It is also possible that the sum of two atoms is strongly atomic, but the supremum of the two summands does not exist. Indeed, let $H:=\ell_{2}^{2}$, so that $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(H\right)$ is strongly atomic by part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{strictstrong}. Let $f:=\left(1,0\right)$ and $g:=\left(0,1\right)$, so that $\left(f,1\right)$ and $\left(g,1\right)$ are atoms in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(H\right)$, their sum is strongly atomic (because every positive vector in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(H\right)$ is), but $\left(f,1\right)$ and $\left(g,1\right)$ do not have a supremum, as $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(H\right)$ is an antilattice (Corollary~\ref{antilattice2}), and $\left(f,1\right)$ and $\left(g,1\right)$ are incomparable.
\qed
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
\label{noocomp}
Let $F:=\left(\ell_{1},\|\cdot\|_{*}\right)$, where $\|\cdot\|_{*}$ is the renorming of $\ell_{1}$ defined by $\|f\|_{*}:=\sqrt{\|f\|_{1}^{2}+\|f\|_{2}^{2}}$. One can show that this norm is strictly convex, which implies that $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$ is strongly atomic according to part~(i) of Proposition~\ref{strictstrong}. Also, since $\|\cdot\|_{2}\le\|\cdot\|_{1}$ on $\ell_{1}$, it follows that $\|\cdot\|_{*}\le\sqrt{2}\|\cdot\|_{1}$.

Let $\left(f_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be the standard basis of $\ell_{1}$, and for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ let $e_{n}:=\left(f_{n},0\right)$. Then, $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is norm bounded in $ 
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$, hence order bounded. Let us show that $\left(e_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ does not have an order Cauchy subnet.

Assume that $\left(e_{n_{\alpha}}\right)_{\alpha\in A}$ is an order Cauchy subnet, witnessed by $P\subseteq  
  \mathord{ 
    \tikz[baseline=-1.2ex,scale=0.13]{
                
      \draw (-1,0) -- (1,0);
                        
      \draw (-1,0) arc (180:0:1);
                     
      \draw (-1,0) -- (0,-2);
      \draw (1,0) -- (0,-2);
    } 
  } 
\left(F\right)$. That is, for every $p\in P$ there is $\alpha_{p}\in A$ such that for every $\beta,\gamma\ge\alpha_{p}$ we have $e_{n_{\beta}}-e_{n_{\gamma}}\le p$. Let us show that $P\ge \left(0_{F},1\right)$, thus immediately reaching a contradiction.

Fix $p\in P$ and let $p=\left(h,r\right)$. Fix $k\in \mathbb{N}$. There is $\beta_{k}\ge\alpha_{p}$ such that $n_{\beta_{k}}\ge k$, and there is $\gamma_{k}\ge\alpha_{p}$ such that $n_{\gamma_{k}}> n_{\beta_{k}}$. Let $g_{k}:=f_{n_{\beta_{k}}}-f_{n_{\gamma_{k}}}$; then $\left(g_{k},0\right)\le p$ yields $\|h- g_{k}\|_{*}\le r$. Since the coordinates of $h$ converge to $0$, it is not hard to show that $\|h- g_{k}\|_{1}\to \|h\|_{1}+2$ and $\|h- g_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\to \|h\|_{2}^{2}+2$. Hence,
\[r^{2}\ge \|h\|_{2}^{2}+2+ \|h\|_{1}^{2}+4+4\|h\|_{1}> \|h\|_{*}^{2}+2\|h\|_{*}+1= \left(\|h\|_{*}+1\right)^{2},\]
implying $r\ge \|h\|_{*}+1$, and so $\left(h,r\right)\ge \left(0_{F},1\right)$, as required.
\qed
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- example-17: body_md -->
\label{megaice}
Let $B$ be the Boolean algebra of clopen sets of the Cantor space $\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{N}}$. Any choice of the first $n$ coordinates gives rise to an element of $B$; we denote the collection of all such elements by $B_{n}$. Clearly, $B_{n}$ consists of $2^{n}$ disjoint nonzero elements which add up to $1_{B}$. Moreover, for every $0_{B}\ne b\in B$ there is $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $b$ is a disjoint union of a finite number of elements of $B_{n}$. 

Let $M:=M\left(B\right)$ be the space of finitely additive real-valued measures on $B$. Note that $M$ is an AL-space with respect to the total variation norm. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\rho_{n}$ be the seminorm on $M$ defined by $\rho_{n}\left(\mu\right):=\sum_{b\in B_{n}}\left|\mu\left(b\right)\right|$. Note that $\rho_{n}\le \rho_{n+1}$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and if $\mu\ge 0_{M}$, then $\rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)=\|\mu\|$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

On $\ell_{\8}\oplus M$ consider the following version of the ice cream cone
\[C:=\left\{\left(f,\mu\right): f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)\text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}\right\}.\]
Since $C$ is closed with respect to pointwise topologies on $\ell_{\8}$ and $M$, the cone $C$ is Archimedean. Let $E$ be $\ell_{\8}\oplus M$ ordered by $C$.

For every $\mu\in M$ we have $\left(\|\mu\|\1,\mu\right)\in C$. It follows that $h:=\left(\1,0_{M}\right)$ is an order unit of $E$. Indeed, for any $f\in\ell_{\8}$ and $\mu\in M$ we have $\pm\left(f,\mu\right)\le \left(\|f\|+\|\mu\|\right)h$.

Let us show that order intervals are directed order compact. In fact, since $E$ is an order unit space, it is enough to show this for $\left[0_{E},h\right]$. Let $\left(f_{\alpha},\mu_{\alpha}\right)_{\alpha\in A}\subseteq \left[0_{E},h\right]$. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha\in A$ we have $1-f_{\alpha}\left(n\right),f_{\alpha}\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu_{\alpha}\right)$; in particular, $0\le f_{\alpha}\left(n\right)\le 1$, and for every $0_{B}\ne c\in B$ there is $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $c$ is the disjoint union of a subset of $B_{n}$, hence $\left|\mu_{\alpha}\left(c\right)\right|\le \rho_{n}\left(\mu_{\alpha}\right)\le 1$.

By passing to a subnet, we may therefore assume that there are functions $f\colon \mathbb{N}\to\left[0,1\right]$ and $\mu \colon B\to\left[-1,1\right]$ such that $f_{\alpha}\left(n\right)\to f\left(n\right)$ and $\mu_{\alpha}\left(b\right)\to \mu\left(b\right)$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $b\in B$.

By continuity, $\mu$ is a measure, and $1-f\left(n\right),f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, hence $e:=\left(f,\mu\right)\in \left[0_{E},h\right]$. It is left to show that $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} e$. First, note that $e-e_{\alpha}\in \left[-h,h\right]$, for every $\alpha$. Hence, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha$ we have $1-\left|f_{\alpha}\left(n\right)-f\left(n\right)\right|\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu_{\alpha}-\mu\right)$.

For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $g_{n}:=\frac{2}{n}\1_{\left[1,n\right]}+\1_{\left[n+1,\8\right)}$ and let $P:=\left\{\left(g_{n},0_{M}\right)\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$. It is easy to see that $P\downarrow 0_{E}$. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is $\alpha_{n}$ such that $\left|f_{\alpha}\left(k\right)-f\left(k\right)\right|\le \frac{1}{n}$, and $\left|\mu_{\alpha}\left(b\right)-\mu\left(b\right)\right|\le \frac{1}{2^{k}n}$, for every $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$, $k=1,\ldots,n$, and $b\in B_{k}$. Let us show that $\left(g_{n},0_{M}\right)\ge \pm\left(e_{\alpha}-e\right)$, for $\alpha\ge\alpha_{n}$. For $k=1,\ldots, n$, we have
\[g_{n}\left(k\right)-\left|f_{\alpha}\left(k\right)-f\left(k\right)\right|\ge \frac{1}{n}=2^{k}\frac{1}{2^{k}n}\ge \rho_{k}\left(\mu_{\alpha}-\mu\right).\]
For $k>n$, we have
\[g_{n}\left(k\right)-\left|f_{\alpha}\left(k\right)-f\left(k\right)\right|=1-\left|f_{\alpha}\left(k\right)-f\left(k\right)\right|\ge \rho_{k}\left(\mu_{\alpha}-\mu\right).\]
We conclude that $P$ witnesses $e_{\alpha}\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{do}} e$.

We now show that $E$ is not atomic. First, if $\mu,\nu\in M_{+}$ are such that $\mu\le\nu$, then $\left(\|\mu\|\1,\mu\right)\le \left(\|\nu\|\1,\nu\right)$. Indeed, for $\lambda:=\nu-\mu\in M_{+}$ we have $\|\lambda\|=\|\nu\|-\|\mu\|$, and so $\left(\|\nu\|\1,\nu\right)-\left(\|\mu\|\1,\mu\right)=\left(\|\lambda\|\1,\lambda\right)\in C$.

Conversely, assume that $\mu\in M$, $\nu\in M_{+}$ and $f\in\ell_{\8}$ satisfy $0_{E}\le \left(f,\mu\right)\le \left(\|\nu\|\1,\nu\right)$. We show that $0_{M}\le \mu\le \nu$ and $f=\|\mu\|\1$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\|\nu\|=1$. Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$. We have $f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)$ and $1-f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\nu-\mu\right)$. Hence,
\[1\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)+\rho_{n}\left(\nu-\mu\right)= \sum\limits_{b\in B_{n}}\left(\left|\mu\left(b\right)\right|+\left|\nu\left(b\right)-\mu\left(b\right)\right|\right)\ge \sum\limits_{b\in B_{n}}\nu\left(b\right)=\nu\left(1_{B}\right)=\|\nu\|=1,\]
and so all present inequalities are in fact equalities. In particular, for every $b\in B_{n}$ we have $\left|\mu\left(b\right)\right|+\left|\nu\left(b\right)-\mu\left(b\right)\right|=\nu\left(b\right)$, hence $0\le \mu\left(b\right)\le \nu\left(b\right)$. We see that $\mu$ and $\nu-\mu$ are positive. Moreover, $f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\mu\right)=\|\mu\|$, and $1-f\left(n\right)\ge \rho_{n}\left(\nu-\mu\right)=\|\nu-\mu\|=1-\|\mu\|$. We conclude that $f\left(n\right)=\|\mu\|$, hence $f = \|\mu\|\1$.

For every measure $\mu\in M_{+}$ which is not atomic there are $\lambda,\nu\in M_{+}$ which are not multiples of $\mu$ and such that $\mu=\lambda+\nu$. It follows that
\[e:=\left(\|\mu\|\1,\mu\right)=\left(\|\lambda\|\1,\lambda\right)+\left(\|\nu\|\1,\nu\right)\]
is a positive decomposition of $e$ into non-proportional positive summands, and so $e$ is not an atom. Assume further that $\mu$ is disjoint with all atomic measures, for example $\mu$ is the Bernoulli measure, which assigns $\mu\left(b\right):=2^{-n}$, for every $b\in B_{n}$. Suppose that $0_{E}\le g\le e$. Then, by the previous step, we have that $g=\left(\|\lambda\|\1,\lambda\right)$, where $0_{M}\le \lambda\le \mu$. In particular, $\lambda$ is atomless, and so $g$ is not an atom. Thus, there are no atoms in $\left[0_{E},e\right]$.
\qed
<!-- end example-17 -->
